utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Welcome back to this trial. Before we have the next witness, there's some procedural matters I would like to inform everybody. This morning we'll hear the last witness left over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we call this Monday phenomenon, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Can you hear me? Yes. Good morning, everybody. Welcome back to this trial. Before we have the witness, there are some scheduling matters I would like to inform everybody. Today we'll hear the last witness left over from the previous group. And according to our plan, we are going to hear Mr. Nikolic on Wednesday. As for the next week's scheduling, next Tuesday, 23rd of September, we'll sit in the morning instead of the afternoon, so the next week the whole morning we'll sit in the morning. We might have a break from 13th of October to 17th of October. Of course, this scheduling all depends on the decisions of the Appeals Chamber. I would like to reiterate the Bench's position on this matter. Whatever the decision the Appeals Chamber may render, this Bench will comply with it. Thank you. Having said that, could we have the witness. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I hope you can hear me, but we're not getting any audio at the moment, so we won't be able to understand Mr. Stojanovic. Also, and if the Court doesn't mind, I will be leaving after the first break, and Mr. Waespi will be leading this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Yes, I can. I think it seems to be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next witness will be Lieutenant Colonel Franken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So there are no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, there is none, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Blagojevic. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to address you, although I was not given the opportunity to take the floor. I would like to just state for the record that I do not have the Defence. These persons who are sitting here today should not be sitting as my Defence, and I would like this to be known. I am in this position: I am in such an unfortunate situation, considering that you have said certain things which I deem to be false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagojevic, I believe that your remarks have been rightly registered in the transcript. We all stand your position at this moment. As I promise you, that we're all waiting for the decisions from the Appeals Chamber, and whatever decisions the Appeals Chamber may render on the issue of the counsel, this Bench will comply with it. Thank you. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hear you pretty well, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Franken.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please state for the record your full name.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'm Robert Alexander Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And perhaps just to remind you and me that we are speaking the same language, although not our native language, but still English. If you could pause after I have asked you a question, and perhaps watch the monitor, and as soon as the cursor has stopped moving, you can answer my question.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That makes is easier for the interpreter. I'll just recount a couple of personal details, and if you could confirm, please. Your nationality is Dutch?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you were born on the 24th of August, 1950?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you're a lieutenant colonel in the Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: An infantry officer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I'll briefly go over your military c.v. You joined the army in 1970 and have held many positions in these 30 years, including the commander of a mechanised armoured -- mechanised infantry company, operations officer in an armoured brigade, officers' tactics instructor at the infantry school, chief of training at an infantry training unit, then staff officer concerned with logistics and intelligence at battalion and brigade levels, and more recently, you were a G-2 - that's a staff officer responsible for intelligence and security of a mechanised brigade - chief of crisis response operations, and currently you are the chief of staff of Northern Command here in Holland?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also trained as an airborne officer, and at the time of the events we are concerned with today, you were the deputy commander of the 1st Dutch UN infantry battalion based in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that detail was from January 1995 to July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now going to this mission you had. Can you briefly describe the mission you had, you were given by your superiors.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, there were three missions. The first one was to deter by presence any hostile action of -- in the enclave. The second was to facilitate humanitarian aid to the civilian population, and the third one was to demilitarise the Bosnian forces in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant Colonel. As a deputy commander, what were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I had to coordinate the work of the battalion staff and act as a commander the moment a commander was not available or not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how did you divide up the duties among yourselves?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, it was that the external contacts was done by Lieutenant Colonel Karremans, and all the internal affairs, so the orders to the battalion and the companies, was my job, part of the job, within the guidelines of the commander, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So the commander, Colonel Karremans, would decide, and you would implement these decisions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said you were responsible for internal matters. Does that also involve logistics?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. My second job as DCO was logistics officer of the battalion, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, where were you normally based?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: My base was Potocari, HQ of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was there a specific room where you conducted your business?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as normal business, it was from my bureau annex, bat room annex, et cetera. It was a small office, and as soon as there was something important, my place was in the operations room of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Judges what happens in an operations room?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, all the information from the battalion is coming in there, is analysed, and on the basis of those analyses, decisions are taken or orders are given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I take it you couldn't be always present in that operations room. How would you make sure that they were still briefed as to the information that came into the operations room?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well my chief operations room had guidelines from my side in which I said information like that I want to know, I want to have, and your analysis about events, I want to have. And in the end phase I was most of the time in the operation room, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, one of the three-fold missions or mandates, you told us a moment ago, was demilitarisation. Now, was that successful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, sir. The two Dutch battalions who were there before us already tried to demilitarise the area. The problem was that we were not authorised to enter civil houses. So what happened if we saw armed men, we tried to catch them, so to say, but the very moment they fled into a house, we were not allowed to enter that house. I have to call in so-called civil police, that's local police, which in a couple of events came out - sorry - came out. We can't find any weapon. And that happened several times. So more or less we stopped trying to catch those guys within a city or within a village because it was absolutely no use. And in fact, only, yeah, a laugh, because the population stood around and laughed broadly when we tried again to pick up some guys who were bebic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, were there still times you were successful in getting arms, weapons; and if so, what would happen to these weapons?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: A couple of times we catch groups of two or three men in the open. The weapons were then handed over to us. They got a receipt and the weapons went to a so-called weapon collection point, on the base of our B Company in the city of Srebrenica there was a WCP or a weapon collection point. And all the weapons that were given over were held there -- were kept there, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were there collected, apart from small arms which you had referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In the period we were there we only collected small arms but there were already T-55 that's a main battle tank. As far as I recollect, two artillery pieces, all kinds of self-constricted weapons. All of them was a rocket parts normally under an armed helicopter or an airplane and they made it on a mount and probably used that as artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you just confirmed a couple of times that the area wasn't really demilitarised, or you were not successful. Now, why did the Muslims not really hand in their weapons? Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I think they still wanted to have their military potential because the Bosnian Serbs around were pretty heavily armed, and they still saw that as a threat. And probably didn't fully believe in what I call the combat power of the Blue Helmet. Our mission was to deter by presentation, so just showing the blue flag, so to say. A little battalion, lightly armed, by a real attack, we were not able to stop it, but not even authorised to stop it in the situation we were in. So I think that out of a wish for self-defence, they kept weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the Muslims who had weapons, what military structure did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: When we came in, it was called the 8th operational group. Later on it was called the 28th division. It was more or less a division structure. They had four brigades. The enclave was divided in four areas, and every brigade had a responsibility for an area. And there were more or less company structures under the brigade, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How would you characterise their organisation? You just mentioned a very detailed or hierarchical structure, divisions, brigades, companies. Was that something just on paper or did it materialise in reality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. It was paper structure. In fact, there was not a consequent line of command. Commanders on low level did exactly what they wanted themselves. They didn't follow orders from the division, et cetera. So to be short, it was a mess, militarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did they have a headquarters at the divisional level?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, they had a headquarters formerly in the so-called post and telegraph office in the city of Srebrenica and there was another headquarters in Potocari, in part of an old school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever visit this headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I know the post and telegraph office. It was not a headquarters but just an office but no communication or maps or whatever. And in fact the same situation was in Potocari. It was a classroom or a room, and there were some bureaus in it but no communications. They had a house in the vicinity of Pale, within the enclave there's a Pale too, and in that house there were communications, means of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you said you visited this headquarters. How many people did you see working there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There were -- on the outside working there, six or seven guys who were present in that room, not really working in the way I see it in a divisional escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you have a discussion with the Chief of Staff of the Bosnian Muslim army at one point in time while you were there about cooperation, so to call it, between DutchBat and their army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I got a question of the Chief of Staff 28th division what DutchBat would do when the Bosnian Serbs would attack the enclave. I explained to him that we were not allowed to defend the enclave, but understanding the importance of the question, we had some strange discussion where I, in the end, we agreed that in the case that Bosnian Serbs would attack the enclave, we would defend our observation post, as far as possible, and they would be in the area between the observation post and defend the enclave. But in a way, that very partially coordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when the scenario of attack eventually happened, did this concept materialise?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In one place, the essence of a concept like that is of course that when one of the parties withdraws, he informs the other party that -- the big problem, the 28th Division, just in one case, informed us in time that they would withdraw, in all the other cases we found ourselves in the midst of the Serb infantry. And they did not inform us. One of the reasons we lost quite a lot of OPs -- sorry, observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to the Bosnian Serb army, iso BSA or whatever you like to call them. Prior to the fall of the enclave, did you have contacts with VRS officers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We had an official liaison. It was a Colonel Vukovic who belonged in a way to the Skelani Brigade. It was on the east and south-east part of the enclave. But in fact we dealt with somebody who presented himself as Major Nikolic, belonging to the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you what his position was within the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, it was a bit difficult, because asked for it, we got all kinds of functions, operations officer, one time he claimed to be DCO, so second in command of the brigade. We were not quite clear what post he had, but it was obvious that he had a post in that way that he could influence the operations of the brigade, because he was the one which we tried to make appointments with, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever see him giving orders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Once Observation Post Papa, in the northern part of the enclave, the entrance to the enclave, where he ordered some soldiers in the vicinity of that entrance to do things, and they did. And the other time was when we had a meeting at the confrontation line directly in the vicinity of Observation Post Romeo. It's on the eastern side of the enclave. Where he gave some orders to the troops in the Serbian line present there, which were followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in this roughly half a year you were there in your capacity, how many times would you meet Major Nikolic prior to the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I understand. I think it will be four or five times, because generally we had a liaison, so-called S-5, whose job it was to keep up the contacts with the VRS or BSA. I should think of the fact that when he negotiated with one of the parties, the S-5, we always kept some echelons in reserve that when he didn't come to a solution, we were still could bring in somebody higher who could try again, and that was what we did. The last phase, in fact, Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Karremans went out, the S-5 didn't succeed. I went out and tried to negotiate whatever. So I think it's about five times that I met him within that situation of negotiations or talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, just to clarify, because most of us are military laymen. What is an S-5?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry, yeah. The situation, the best thing that you could describe it as a liaison to a party. And that's in fact the best description I can give for the function he has now. Normally he does civil, military cooperation as well, but it was not applicable in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, to summarise: These meetings you had with Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic, these were liaison meetings, where things of mutual interest were discussed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. The two times I met him was on request of my own S-5. He said, well, this is going forward, there has to be a bit more brass on the ground, so to say. I remember that in the situation in Romeo, so on the eastern side, it was concerned OP Echo, Observation Post Echo. It was quite a critical point and Serbs had quite a lot of problems with the area. That's where I went in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again, by Romeo, you mean observation point R, Romeo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, sorry. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No problem. Now, did you ever see the commander of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you expect, would you have expected to see the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, given the fact that you had dealings with the liaison person on the other side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. There were some situations in which I was surprised that we still had to deal with Major Nikolic. And there was a situation with the proposition of trade with the enclave from the Serb side. It was pretty important, but the level never got higher in beginning as Major Nikolic. Later on somebody from Pale came in. And the Echo situation, it was pretty critical, I should say I was surprised that I found Major Nikolic on the CL. Colonel Vukovic was there as well but not on commander level. I know that Colonel Karremans a couple of times requested to speak with the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, but it was -- contact never came, you say, never got effective.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you ever receive complaints by the Serb side about any issue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. There are two examples, two issues I remember. There was probably an action of the Muslims, Bosniaks, directly north of the Observation Post Mike, M, where my OP reported what we call battle noise by night on the Serb side, and saw in the morning smoke behind the hill, probably -- yeah, something of burning. That's where I got a complaint through the S-5 of the Serb side that the Muslims did perform a raid and burnt houses and killed people. And the second I remember was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you can just stop for a moment. I would like you to point to a map just to make it more graphic, and if you could be shown Exhibit P21.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's an exhibit which has been used several times before. And we need to use the old-fashioned way, the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, if you could point out, as soon as it starts to work, the observation point Mike you discussed a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Is this the correct overlay? I see Zvornik on it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. You need to move down more into southerly direction.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mike was in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you can point to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Mike was in this area, northern point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe you point to the area where we see the village of Jaglici.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the area. Their observation was somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, going back to what you said, you heard about the allegations of the Serb person who complained to you. Did you try to verify that it was true that the Muslims performed a raid and burnt houses and killed people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We had the probability that they had by the report of OP Mike, Observation Post Mike, but we were not allowed to go on the very spot to check it out ourselves. They didn't want us to operate or to come out of the enclave. And they, I mean Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe you may have said that, but what was the time when this incident happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That must be -- let me think. I suppose around April. Sorry. It's eight years ago, so the correct date, I don't know. But it must have been around April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you started with a second incident.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. There was an incident south of Zeleni Jadar. There was a route used by the Bosniaks to go to Zepa, and somewhere in that area, the Bosnian Serb army claimed that the Bosniaks ambushed a couple of their soldiers, and as I remember well, seven of them were -- seven of them were killed. You see here in the south Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could again point to the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Here is Zeleni Jadar. And in this area, going from here, there was a route they used to Zepa. So somewhere in the area directly south of the map that ambush would have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you can leave it there. We may use it again. In this instance, did you again try to verify whether the information relayed to you was correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we got a complaint about two days after the incident happened, so there was no use in checking any more, because probably the bodies, et cetera, would be taken away, and then you can't see anything in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you couldn't --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I couldn't check that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember a date?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I'll do my best. I think this happened after the raid of the Muslims in the north, so probably that would be end of April, starting May, sir. But again, I don't recollect the correct or just exactly a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that would be, of course, April/May 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Turning to the other side, were there complaints by the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Several -- the problem was, in fact, that there were three confrontation lines, three borders of the enclave. There was a UN border, there was the Bosnian Serb border, was more or less one or two kilometres further -- within the enclave; and there was a Bosniak border, which was locally one or two kilometres further outside the UN border. So every time we got a complaint that the Serbs came forward, it was a bit difficult to discuss that, because nobody agreed on the UN border. In fact, we had a couple of incidents where it was obvious that the Bosnian Serbs came forward. It was once in the east, directly south of the Observation Post Romeo, where the Serbs came forward just to the road that went to Romeo. Just hold, please. Being in this area. There's a road from Srebrenica up here, and Quebec and Romeo, both of the observation posts, were alongside that road. And between Romeo and the city, the Serbs came forward, so controlled that road on the very edge of it. We opposed that and they withdrew. We had a problem in the north and west part. This part where the Serbs came forward. But it was before DutchBat 3 was in, as it appeared on DutchBat 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And just for the record, the witness, in relation to the last piece of information he gave, pointed to the area west of the village of Jaglici and Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. And we had a problem in what we called the Bandera Triangle, here around OP Bravo, where two or three times was reported that the Serbs would have come forward. The first time it was in the period that DutchBat 2 and 3 were in their takeover. The second time was in March, when Serb infantry was reported within the enclave. We counted that but it was a false report, there was no Serb infantry in the enclave. We kept a new position in the area during about two weeks, to make sure they wouldn't come in. And that's about it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned DutchBat 1 and 2. What time frame were they involved in?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, in 1994, the DutchBat 1 was in the first half, so, say, January to July and DutchBat 2 was July up to January 1995, when we relieved them, or switched tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you, Lieutenant Colonel Franken take any complaints to Major Nikolic; and if so, in what instances would you do that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In general, there was a big problem to reach -- no - to get contact, because he just showed up when he wanted. Once in a while we were in need of liaison because villages were shelled, et cetera, and we wanted of course to discuss that, or to report that, or to confront the Bosnian Serb army with it, but then Major Nikolic was not available. That's a general complaint. Specific complaints on the person, I do not have, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you still be more specific about the shelling of these villages?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mostly it was done in the area of the Milici Brigade, in the western part of the enclave, and, for instance, the village of Slatina was several times targeted. And Slatina is, yeah, not on this map, but you should say it's directly east of OP alpha, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the time frame you're talking about would be?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The whole period, sir. I don't need to say that they were constantly shelled, but those incidents were often in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I would like Your Honours to turn to the 11th of July. And I think at that time you were in the operations room in Potocari. Do you recall what type of information you received?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: On the 11th, I got reports of almost all my observation posts that it was very much battle noise from the B Company specifically. B Company was the company where the city of Srebrenica within his area of responsibility and his own base was there. I was reported that there was a pretty heavy shelling of the city of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Could you identify where you told what kind of weapons were used to shell the city?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Probably medium calibre and heavy calibre artillery and mortar, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were you given information as to the numbers of shells that fell on the city?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was standard procedure that every shelling was reported in detail to the battalion by a patrol or an observation post. But when the B Company came to the figure of 200 on that day, I told him to stop reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you form an opinion why the city of Srebrenica was shelled?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. The problem was that the city was absolutely full of civilians, women, children, et cetera. It was absolutely crowded. There were no military positions of the 28th Muslim Division any more there. The only positions there were were our positions, so-called blocking positions. But there was a, yeah, more or less random shelling of the city. The reasons for that can only be, as far as we could figure out, try to panic the population or just to kill the population. And the other -- we couldn't figure out another goal for an action like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when you received this information about the situation in Srebrenica and you were in Potocari, did you give any orders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, the situation there was that we had order to -- got that on the evening of the 9th, to defend the city. But during the 11th, there was a panic and the civil population, let's say the refugees, they overran the HQ of B Company, so I ordered the commander of the B Company to put his HQ means in his APC - armoured personnel carrier - and he had to command his company from there. And in fact we left the base as he said that he couldn't control it any more because our APCs as well were crowded by the people. The climb on our APCs were in position in the field. Massively with positions of my soldiers. The situation was not controllable by him any more. He asked permission to divert, so to say, the refugees to Potocari in the direction of Potocari. I granted that and he made a patrol taking the lead and taking people along to our HQ Potocari. His mission stayed forward, stayed in the blocking positions, and keep the Serbs out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Why would you tell him to keep the Serbs out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That was my -- those were my orders, to defend the city. Although I had to say the very moment that the population went on their march to Potocari, and Serb infantry came on in the back of my company, B Company, they were on the high grounds west and east of Srebrenica. I ordered him to fall back on the back of the column of refugees and keep the Serb -- stay between the Serbs and the refugees until Potocari, and he had to take a position from south in the edge of Potocari. The general idea was to make the area, I had to control with my little means, as small as possible, and in fact to gain time then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me first clarify a couple of things. You said that they were on the high grounds west and east of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: They is infantry of the Bosnian Serb army, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you only said -- you also said that they had to fall on the back of the column of refugees.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That is B Company, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, why did you tell him to be between the civilians and the Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The civilian population was in great fear. They were very afraid of the Serbs. We didn't know how Serb infantry would react when they could penetrate without any control those masses of refugees. I analysed that my mission to defend Srebrenica in that phase meant try to protect the civilian population, because defending an empty city is nonsense, and that's why I ordered him to stay in between him and keep the Serbs away, if necessary, with fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were they forced, in fact, to use fire?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In the blocking positions, they were, by simple fact that my eastern positions were fired at by T-55s, by tanks. My -- correction. My western positions, I should say, were fired at by a tank, a T-55, which was out of reach from my anti-tank weapons, the few that I had. And I know that two APCs fired at the tail of the column on overhead Serb infantry when they tried to approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, for the arrival of the inflowing civilians in Potocari, were arrangements made for the arrival itself, but also for their accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. We had, I suppose it was in the night from the 10th or the 11th already a move by civilians from the city. That was reported to me by patrols. And I ordered the compound commander, Major Otter, who was base commander in Potocari, to reci a safe route into the direct vicinity of our HQ. You should know our HQ was at point blank of Serb artillery, which was posted in the area of Observation Post Papa, in the north.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could be shown the next exhibits, and that is, Your Honour, Exhibit P51. If you could tell us the route that was arranged by Major Otter, the safe route, as you called it, for the civilians.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: This is the road from Bratunac to Srebrenica. In this area, south of the map, in fact, there was high ground on which Serb artillery, two tanks and a multiple launchers, rockets, were posted, who had absolute sight until here. After that, they couldn't see what happened on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you are pointing just to the area on the road right of Feros building?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There's a small band in the road and after that they couldn't see exactly what was on the road. So Major Otter made a route through a bus compound under cover of what's called the blue factory. He made a hole in the fence here and that's where the people came in, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to make things clear: The UN base, can you outline the defence of the UN base?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The white line, this is the fence of the UN base, and our headquarters, this one. It was a right -- yeah. More or less a square area of a former battery factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again the reason why you had a special way for the refugees to get into the compound, in fact you created a new entrance. What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The fact that they were pretty massively shelled at in the city of Srebrenica, we were expecting that the Serbs would open fire the very moment they saw that mass coming down the road. We were warned by the Serbs that they wouldn't tolerate that we took refugees in our base. So those two things together made me take no risk and say: Okay. Try to find out a covered road, as covered as possible. And covered is relatively, because here on the high grounds here on the left side, the Serbs were also there. But they were there only by small arms, with small arms, Serb infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said a moment ago that you were warned by the Bosnian Serbs. Can you tell us more about this warning?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. The warning was again -- came in by radio, because in that phase they had about -- what was it? - 50 POWs, the crews of the observation post held in Bratunac, and they had of course their vehicles as well. And one of our NCOs had to read a text in English that they would not tolerate the refugees coming on the base that they did want in effect just hold a couple of -- and this was repeated after the one close air support mission again that if there was close air support again, again the warning that they would shell the compound, the base, HQ, and the civilians being in the buildings around the compound, this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just two points for clarification purposes. An NCO, that's --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Non-commissioned officer, a sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the second point: You said that if there was close air support again they would shell the compound. So there was close air support, and who would do that against whom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand. We had at least, I should say, some closed air support south of the city of Srebrenica, around 1300 hours on the 11th of July. That was the reason or the trigger for the last message in fact from the Serbs, where they threatened to kill our soldiers, the POWs. They threatened to massively shell the area on this photo as UN base and directly south of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the organisation who would implement this close air support would be which organisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact it was NATO on request of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when the Serbs said, and I quote you, threatened to kill our soldiers and massively shell the area on this photo, did you take that threat seriously at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I didn't believe that they would kill our soldiers, because that would have an impact, but they could use them as they did before as a human shield. That's the biggest threat, as far as I could see, on that very moment for our soldiers. But a threat in the direction of the civil population was much larger, much more impressive, because they did before. And very shortly after that message came there was a, what I say, a kind of devastation by a full layer of rockets fired by their multiple rocket system on the area of Potocari. So it was a serious threat, at least that's how we estimated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned that the closed air support that they threatened if there was another closed air support they would shell again. Was there another closed air support?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who decided that there wouldn't be any more?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The very situation that we came to so-called small area, and I mean the area of our UN base, Potocari, and the buildings directly south of it, there was no use, because the very moment we went on the move from Srebrenica and went to the smaller area, our military options were ended. You can't have close air support in a situation like that, with line of sight of about 400, 500 metres, max, and then try to operate with fixed wing airplanes, so close to a massive concentration of civilians, is not possible. But it was of no use as well because we understood at the very moment that we came back to Potocari that our military options ended. I had about 150 combat trained soldiers, that's all I had, and about 16 per cent of my ammunition for anti-tank ammunition it was even less. So I didn't even have the means to start a fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me briefly return to the exhibit which is on the ELMO. How many refugees were there on the compound inside or outside?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. We concentrated them in this building, which you see in the middle of our base. There was a big hole, more or less. And we had about 5.000 refugees there, sir, and the other 25.000 to 30.000 were in buildings marked on this photograph, here, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: All the buildings who have names like express compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah and the small buildings in between. So in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, just going back to what you said earlier about your means: With your means available and just the situation as you had outlined it before about the military option, which was no longer available to you, did you still consider to take a stand against the VRS or BSA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We considered it. But my possible defensive positions were about 20 metres away from that crowd I described to you before. The very moment we started shooting or firing from that position, we were convinced of the fact that the losses within the crowd would be massive. And if mission then is to protect the civil population. You are not performing -- not executing your mission, of course, but -- because in fact you do the opposite that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you outlined the means you had available at your side. Do you know how much weaponry, what kind of weaponry, was on the side of the Bosnian Serb army at that moment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't know exactly the number of soldiers, of course, but what we call hardware, so artillery and tanks, we had contact with about -- just checking - well, eight main battle tanks, not at the same time, but consequently; and we counted up to 32 artillery positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to move on to the next day, that's the 12th of July. Now, can you tell me, Lieutenant Colonel Franken, what was the first significant event that took place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: On a meeting the night before, so on the evening of the 11th of July, General Mladic told Colonel Karremans that it would be a ceasefire until 10.00 on the 12th, and Colonel Karremans was more or less ordered to be at 10.00 in Bratunac, in a hotel where Mladic wanted to discuss or coordinate further on for the things to happen. The moment 10.00 end of ceasefire, there was a deployed infantry attack supported by tanks from the area, Observation Post Papa, directly aimed -- yeah, it's not on the map, but alongside this road, in the direction of our HQ, in the area of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: From south or north?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: From north to south, sir. From the area Bratunac, in the direction alongside the road to Srebrenica, in the direction of our base and the small -- more or less very directly south of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said there was an infantry and a tank element. How did that attack appear to you? Was it coordinated? Was it disciplined, or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was very -- it was disciplined, absolutely. It was more disciplined as we saw before from the Bosnian Serb army. They were dressed in uniforms, in the very sense of the word, they all had the same uniform. It was obviously a coordination between the tank and the company, the infantry company. So that it looked like a demonstration, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the size --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Company size.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Company size. Now, how did it proceed, this attack? Did it end at one point? And perhaps you can refer to the exhibit which is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: They came deployed to the northern part, so in this area, and then lined up and proceeded their attack until here, where they were stopped by a red and white type, which we used as a boundary for the area where the refugees were in. They stopped there. They didn't go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you just pointed to the area between the "White House" and the blue factory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. A bit farther south, sir, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: North of the Feros building --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: South.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. And you pointed earlier from the southern side, at least of this picture, up north, on the right side of the rectangle or called UN base?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, at what time did this company reach the red/white tape?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It should have been around 11.00, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did Colonel Karremans return; and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He returned, started to debrief me about the things discussed or said during the meeting with Mladic. He didn't -- couldn't finish that, because then the first buses and trucks appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell me what he debriefed you of? What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That it was agreed upon that the Bosnian Serb army would perform the -- what was called the evacuation of the population at that very moment. We were supposed to -- he had contact with the UN HQ, and I suppose it was Sarajevo, in which we were ordered to, yeah, to make sure that the evacuation was performed in a humanitarian, correct way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a time given indicated at what time the evacuation, as you called it, would commence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. What he told me was that as of 1500 hours that afternoon, the evacuation would start, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What you said a moment ago that while you were talking, some buses arrived already.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just buses or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Buses and trucks, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you have contacts with somebody who was part of this evacuation from the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: At the very moment they appeared the first not, not, but later on I had. Colonel Karremans met in the area outside the UN base, General Mladic, on his request, and he said that a colonel would be -- Colonel Adamovic [sic] would be responsible for the evacuation of the population. And I was ordered, being the logistics officer as well of the battalion, to coordinate possible support to the Serbs. And I went out and met that colonel there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that the buses had arrived. What time was that, approximately? You indicated Karremans came back and you started to talk.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It should be somewhere around 12.00, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you recall the discussion you had with this Colonel Adamovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me for transport. He asked me for diesel, diesel I didn't have. The diesel situation was from the very beginning of our mission absolutely disastrous. I was not willing to give him UN vehicles for the evacuation, because he wanted Serb drivers on it. Anyway, and he was not happy with the thought that UN vehicles of DutchBat would be driving around like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was there a time that you eventually gave fuel to the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was after the evacuation had ended, when the first logistic convoy from our logistic base, Busovaca, in the area of Tuzla, so the other Bosniak area. I was ordered to give them diesel appropriate to their use of diesel. So we made a quick count, and as I remember well, we -- the orders came from the UN Sarajevo to give them diesel. And I gave them about 27.000 litres of diesel, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you recall when that happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It must have been in the 15th or 16th of July, one of these days, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when did the "evacuation" end?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The 14th. So they drove with diesel of their own, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And vehicles from -- you also said you wouldn't give them your vehicles, so all the vehicles were from the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Most of them were civil vehicles, sir. Whether they were from Bosnian Serb origin or whatever, I don't know. But were all civilian cars and buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, as we heard about your c.v., you're an experienced logistics officer and served in several functions in brigade staffs. At what level was Colonel Adamovic working?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I understood that he was a G-4 - sorry - logistics officer from Pale. So that would mean the Bosnian Serb headquarters, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And with military terms, talk about units. Did you form an opinion at what level this evacuation needed to be coordinated?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. At least corps level or higher, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly what coordination that was needed to implement this evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you have an evacuation like that, short term, on I'm saying, let's say, 48 hours, and you have transport units within your army, it's pretty easy to do that, because you just give orders to the battalion commanders and they go with all their transport in that direction and perform their job. But I think it's a pretty massive problem if you have to order a concentration of all kinds of civil vehicles, because they're all kinds of factories, et cetera, et cetera, or business partners, more or less to say, where you have to more or less hold the country, you have to concentrate all your bus and truck capacity to perform a job like that. And that is a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In your opinion, how smooth or difficult was the evacuation process, as it was organised by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it went, on the logistics side, it went very smooth, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, we just heard what was arranged in relation to these evacuations and that the buses went ahead. Now, what did you do? What did you decide in relation to these evacuations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, we had to -- the situation was that we were not in control any more. The only thing we could do is to try to influence, as good as we -- as massive as we could. So the very moment the buses and trucks appeared, I ordered my option to make sure that those buses were escorted. We tried in the very beginning to get a man, a Dutch alder on every bus, but that was not possible in every way. There were about 35.000 people to transport. And I would have lost my battalion within half a day, because all the soldiers stepping on the buses and I wouldn't have anybody for the security of the location themselves. I mean, where the rest of the refugees stayed. So I grabbed more or less two officers who were present. It was my S-5, infantry, Major Boering and I put him in a jeep and said stay the hell with that convoy, whatever happens and wherever they go because I wanted to know what happened and I wanted to try to control on the way down to Kladanj, because we knew they were going to the CL in the surroundings of Kladanj. And in that way, try more or less to influence or control the situation. After that, I ordered a captain of mine, Captain Melchers, to organise an escort and the general idea was that with every convoy, at least one jeep with an NCO and soldier in front and one jeep at the tail, to try to make sure that the whole convoy arrived at this mounting point at the CL at Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What actually happened to these escorts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the first three, four convoys went well. After that, it was absolutely first rate. All kinds of reasons. Bosnian Serb army stopped our escorting vehicles with the reason that they were responsible for the safety of the UN soldiers and it was too dangerous down the road to go there for them, so they were stopped. Buses went on. They were stopped and robbed by parts of the Bosnian Serb army, and that went as far -- a couple of my escort teams came back literally in their underpants, vehicle gone, weapons gone, all equipment gone. When the weapons were stolen massively, and I ordered them to go without a weapon. But it didn't work. We were stopped, vehicles were robbed, the guys were robbed, and every time it was not possible to defend themselves. If there were two guys in a jeep in the midst of BSA country and when you're stopped by 20 or 25 armed men, you know, you can't do a thing. So the escort of the convoys went wrong. We didn't actually escort them. We were not able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said you were given an explanation that the Bosnian Serb army was concerned about the security. Did you have -- did you believe that or did you form your own opinion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Safety for the UN soldiers and I was wondering why you send down buses with women and children, same route, safe for them then as well. One of my officers used that argument. But they were stopped and I think it was more an excuse to, yeah, keep their hands free. No witnesses, no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many vehicles overall you lost during this escorting mission?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: About 16 up to 18 vehicles, sir, during the escort mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Jeeps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also said that DutchBat soldiers were -- their equipment was taken away. How many weapons were taken away from your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In total, if I look to the OP crews as well, it must be about 100 small arms, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you had contact with senior VRS officers. You mentioned a few names. Did you complain about that to any of these or other people you haven't mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: My first contact was with Colonel Adamovic as I described before, but later on there came a Colonel Jankovic, who was said to be responsible for DutchBat and the leaving of DutchBat out of the enclave. And I complained to him several times about this. He said every time that he would go in for it, he would arrange it and give me a list of which vehicles, et cetera. But nothing happened, in fact. And one of the last times I requested, I said, yeah, we have a small problem because the BSA is not an army like your army. I can't control all militia, et cetera. So we're doing our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What kind of person was this Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, he was -- he at least looked like a soldier, a professional soldier, seeing his dress. It was not so very common that members of the BSA walked around in proper uniform. He did. He kept far away or held himself far away from anything to do with evacuation or deportation. He repeatedly said: No, that's not my job. I'm not considered -- I'm just here for the retreat of DutchBat. But he -- I have an example that he had quite some influence. Perhaps we come to it, but I still had in the end 59 wounded, civil wounded, within the compound, and Serbs told me that it was no problem. DutchBat could go, just hand the wounded over to the Serbs. They had hospitals as well. Which we refused and said DutchBat is not going anywhere. As long as those wounded are not in safety. We tried all kinds of things. Normedcoy, a medical unit which was part of the sector north-east part of UNPROFOR, UN unit, tried to come down to us to get the wounded out, which failed because they were massively shot at during the route through BSA area, BSA country. And then through MSF, Medecins Sans Frontieres, I got contact through the ICRC and they came down on the 17th of July to pick up the wounded. There was a problem because they brought in as well medical supply, and the truck with the medical supply was stopped by the Serbs at the border at Zvornik. The lady in charge of the ICRC mission complained to him about that, and it was -- I was more or less surprised that he took out a handy, a telephone, called a number, said something - what he said, I don't know, because I don't understand Croatian - and with a smile, he said: The truck is coming down. So probably -- obviously he was able to order things to Serb boundary trips, border trips.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you make a comment to him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I said to him: Well, that's quite something for a Bosnian Serb colonel to order Serb border troops. And he didn't react. He smiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he tell you at one time where he was living?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He told me he lived in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in what language would you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Beginning, through an interpreter, a Serb. Later on it proved that he spoke English and we had discussions in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me turn back to Potocari. And we are still on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Waespi, how long do you think you could finish your direct examination? If less than ten minutes, you may continue. If not, I think it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. No. It will be more than ten minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll break now and we'll resume until 15 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if there other things that the parties would like for bring to the attention of this Bench, we'll have our witness. I said if there's no other things. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry, Ms. Usher, to occupy again. If the witness could be shown Exhibit P80, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's the man I know as Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And incidentally, you talked about the colonel that was in charge of logistics as pointed out by Colonel Karremans, and you called him Adamovic, I believe. Could it also be Acamovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that could be so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now let me turn back to Potocari and the refugees. Can you tell the Judges, and we are now in the afternoon of the 12th of July, the state of the refugees at this time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. People itself were, yeah, you could say living dead. I think the correct word is lethargic. They didn't react. Once in a while there was something like panic but always shortly and they -- completely. They were not interested in whatever and not even in each other, because the situation was, let's say, very grave for the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, how do you know? Did you make tours around the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Now I at least twice a day I made a round through the compound and the area outside, just to keep in touch with reality. Because if you lock yourself up in an OPs room you get reports but it's never complete in the way that you have to sense what happens and see for yourself what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How can you describe the hygienic conditions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was a disaster, sir. For instance, in the building on our base, there were about 5.000 refugees. People were too afraid to go outside to use a toilet or something like that. So they let everything run on the very spot. For instance, when I made my round, I met one woman who was in labour, was getting a baby, and one and a half metres from there were people sitting or using the floor as a toilet. It was quite disastrous.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So they weren't in a position to help each other?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I think they could have been in the position, but they didn't have the means. But they were mentally broken, so to say. They didn't react on each other, hardly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, was there a time that a group of soldiers tried to enter the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. It was on the 12th, shortly after the attack I described from the area of observation point Papa, of that military unit, so to say. There were about 15 militia-like men on a gate, a not-used gate of the base, and that group was swelling up to about 40 who wanted to enter the base and said to my guards over there that they wanted to inspect the base whether there were Muslim military units present on our base.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If Madam Usher could please show him again Exhibit P51. If you could identify for the Judges the location where the group of soldiers tried to enter.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was in here, by this gate, directly north of the building you see here, white, what we call blue factory. That's -- we have another blue factory on this photograph, but this building was where our HQ and support company was stationed. And directly north of it you see that little white road there, was a gate, that was closed, and they wanted to enter there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you allow them to enter?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes and no. That's not an answer, of course, but I went there myself and asked for a commander, or anybody who spoke English or something like that, and there was a soldier or a soldier-like type who spoke English. And out of this group, somebody stepped forward and said he was the commander. I said: You're not going to enter in this mess. In the meantime there were some men with dog who came to that same group. I said: You're not going to enter like that. What we could do is the commander can join me and we can walk over to the base to see whether there are military units. The reason for that was that I wanted to prevent seeing the location and the vulnerability of my refugees that they started to fight or started shooting like that. So I took the commander and the men and took a quick round of the base. I let them in this -- there was an entrance here in the hall. They had a quick overview of the refugees in the base floor -- no, not base floor. The first floor, it is called. And then I took them out and brought them out again and closed the gate again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: For how long were they inside?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: All together, two or three minutes, absolutely not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And can you describe the uniforms these soldiers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. A lot of them were -- the most of them had a combination of all kinds of military clothing, so it looked like militia that were guys with bandannas over their head. But there were five or six in dark uniforms, uniforms that were comparable with the uniforms the Serbian border troops wore, that black and blue, that dark uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the dogs, what kind of dogs were those?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: German shepherds, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you hear at any time that Mladic was in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. My commander -- there was not a unit, but the commander in this area, first lieutenant, reported that Mladic came to the red and white type and addressed the refugees. He wanted to enter, but that was refused to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the refugees: Inside the compound, how many refugees were there all together?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Later on we discovered -- more or less we discovered that about 5.000 of them were there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were these children, women, men?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There were a couple of men, but the mass was women, children, and elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many men were inside the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I could be pretty accurate about that, because probably we'll come to that, but I had the men registered and on the list it said 239, but it was bad counting on my side. 251 men registered and there were about 60 or 70 who refused to be registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And outside the compound how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was very difficult but on the basis of the number of buses et cetera that left, we reckoned that there were about 30.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And again, was it the majority children and women?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many men would you estimate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We estimated that about 600, 700 men were amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to these men, these 600, 700 people. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Afterwards I heard what happened to them, but at the very moment that the evacuation proceeded, Mladic had said that he wanted to interrogate the men in the age of 16 up to 60, because they were potential soldiers. And whether to check, as he called it, whether there were war criminals in between them. And then they -- when they were not war criminals, they would be sent out to Kladanj as well. So they were separated from the rest, the very moment they came out of our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did that appear to you as a reasonable request?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, well, it is -- the procedure as it is is a normal procedure. It's the same what we learn our soldiers. If you have a big group of prisoners, then you start separating them, women, children, and potential combatants. And if you have the combatants, on the basis of their uniform, you divide them again in ranks. So the fact that he wanted to check whether between the men there were BiH soldiers is, according to international law, normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said they were separated. Do you know where they were taken to, to what location?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. They were separated and brought to what is on this photograph as the "White House", this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you try to ascertain what happened to these men?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. The very moment that we discovered that they were brought there, I -- although I couldn't order them, I ordered our -- the present UNMOs, United Nations military observers, to check, to go to the house and check how many men went in, how many went out, and what happened to them. They did that, and in the beginning we had the same numbers going in and the same numbers going out. And they came out. They were transported in a -- what we call a blue -- it was actually a blue bus. And in the beginning, that bus went along with the refugee convoys and it had our escort's specific interest at -- that stayed. But as I told you before, the escort, the actual escorting of those convoys, failed completely by obstruction by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know in what area your escort lost contact with this blue bus?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, several times we already missed him in Bratunac. As long as the escort more or less functioned, we lost him in Bratunac already. Because it's a giant problem. You're going away with about, let's say, 40, 50 vehicles, one vehicle of my battalion in front and one at the edge. And then going through a village or city with all bans, et cetera, it's almost impossible to control where buses are, or stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, these prevention of your escorts, did that appear to be a random occurrence or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. The first time it happened I thought it was in fact the militia who didn't follow orders or something like that. But it was an absolute habit and it existed as of the late afternoon of the 12th, in fact. All my escorts were obstructed for all kinds of reasons, or even, as I told you before, robbed and left in their underpants in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what do you mean by an absolute habit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, all my escorts were stopped. It was not an incident any more, but none of them came further than the Kabala area. Kabala, that's a village somewhere halfway down to Kladanj. They didn't go through anymore. They were stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So did you form an opinion as to whether there was a policy behind stopping your escorts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. When it was -- all the escorts were stopped, it was clear that must have been some order in the base of it, as the basic reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the witness, please, could be shown Exhibit P75.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall this building?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. This building is the "White House", sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what happened in the white house?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In the beginning, and I mean in the beginning of 12, afternoon, they were lead and they were interrogated. I sent patrols down as well to check that. And it went relatively normal. But the violence and intimidation of those men increased rapidly during the later afternoon of the 12th. It went that far that we were not able to send down patrols because we were stopped by Serb soldiers in the amount and the number far outnumbering our numbers, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what could you say that the intimidation of those men increased?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sounds in the last reports of the UNMO, sir. Yelling. We heard shouts, that was at the time the UNMOs were there. Those men came out in numbers. So that's sounds we heard, yelling, crying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was that in accordance with these procedures you had explained earlier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, sir. Normally when you're a POW, the only thing you have to do is name your rank, your name, your registration number, and that's it. You can't be -- and you may not be forced to give more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you know what happened to their personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. They had to lay down their personal belongings when they entered the house, which, as it is, is normal as well. But as I recollect it, on the morning of the 14th, their personal belongings were all set afire and burnt, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit P77, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you have seen this picture before. Can you tell us what you see on it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I see a pile of personal belongings here, beginning of the road to the "White House". And they were set afire, I saw it myself as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And it's probably not easy to tell where the "White House" is. Do you know where it is or hides, just approximately.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It should be somewhere here, because that is as far as I recollect. The northern part of the electric station. On the other exhibit you called -- you pointed out an electrical station. But as I see it, that's the electrical station, somewhere around here, the white house, just behind the trees.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the witness earlier pointed to the white shadow form in the middle of the picture, the top picture, that yellow tarmac or sand, and then pointed to the left of it, between the power mast and that white shape.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry to cut in. I saw some words on the top of the picture. Could somebody help us to translate it into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. President. I apologise. I should have mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Since you are probably the only person in this courtroom who speaks Dutch, could you tell us what it says on the top of the picture?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's to -- by witness J.H.A. Rutten, who was in the battalion, made available photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Franken, you said that the -- you did send patrols to the "White House" and they couldn't enter. Did you form an opinion why they were prevented?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, again it was obvious that they didn't want to have witnesses for the things going on in the "White House". Otherwise I can't imagine a reason why you should stop patrols of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
