utterances.text: Now, I believe on the 12th, again July 1995, you talked to Ibro Nuhanovic. Do you remember a conversation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this was about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhanovic was one of the three representatives of the refugees, so he was part of the committee. And he wanted to speak to me. I spoke to him in my office. And he said that I had to stop the evacuation. Before we already considered that, to stop it, but, as I explained to Mr. Nuhanovic, in fact he gave me the choice between, as I numbered it then, 25.000 women and children, and as far as we could see, 700 men, and that we chose for the 25.000 women and children. We had a short discussion. He said that he understood me, not that he had the same point of view, but he understood me, and left, I mean left my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said that he was one of the three representatives of the refugees and he was part of the committee.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What role did this committee play?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Then I have to go back to the evening of the 11th. As I recollect, 8.00, 2000 hours, there was the first meeting between Colonel Karremans and Mladic, in Bratunac, and on that he ordered the next meeting at 10.00 or 11.00. And he wanted the leadership of the enclave being present. The leadership of the enclave wasn't there. Civilian leaders and the military leaders had left the enclave or were busy leaving the enclave. The 28th Division had started to break out in the area -- to the area of Tuzla in the night of the 10th to the 11th. So they were gone. Then we tried to get a kind of committee from the present civilian population and so we came to three persons, and one of those persons was Mr. Ibrahim Nuhanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And another person would have been -- do you remember another person at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lady whose name I lost again. And Mandzic

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's return to the men. And you had told us what happened to the men who were outside the compound. Did you take a decision in relation to the men who were inside the compound?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was the same decision, in fact. The very moment that I would concentrate the men and let them not go out, I actually stopped the evacuation. Our situation with the refugees was pretty bad. I already described the hygienic situation around, but when the end phase started I had about two-day rations for my own battalion. That means food for about 800 men. I didn't have any fuel, so I wasn't able to purify water to an extent for a mass like this, mass crowd like this. Sorry. I checked out with my medics. I didn't have medical support enough. I didn't have medical supplies enough, and the situation was bad. The people were in bad shape. I checked with one of my medics and said: Okay. Seeing the temperature, seeing the hygienic situation, how long can we hold these people, keep them alive? And he said: Three or four days, and then you have killings or dead by exhaustion, water, lack of water, et cetera. So I wasn't having made a choice for the women and children. I had to proceed with that evacuation to get them out as soon as possible. And I couldn't first said making -- having made the choice already for the women and children instead for the men. Although we tried all kinds of things. I tried to make UN IDs so we could give all kind -- as much as possible, men and let -- that they could prove that they were UN personnel. Because they would go out free. We didn't have the means for it, not to make anything that was a look alike. Then we tried, the well-known list. In fact, it was a trick. I remembered amnesty international used once in a while when there were anonymous prisoners or people in distress, they would try to give them a name or a face. So that's the reason why I had those men registered. We tried to register them outside our base, but that failed because the committee and the interpreters were intimidated by Bosnian Serb soldiers, in a way -- in that way that they didn't have the nerve to go out of our base any more. And that was a problem, because we couldn't communicate with those people. Nobody of us spoke Croatian. Yeah. So, and that was the end, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Exhibit P76, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could put the first page on the ELMO. And can you explain what this means.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I had the committee, which I mentioned before. They were registering the men in that critical age, where year of birth, name, first name, and location of birth were given. In that way, I hoped to give them an identity. I counted at least, and I -- by facsimile, I sent it to my higher echelon, which means to the HQ of sector north-east, in fact, my direct commander within the UN structure. I faxed it to Sarajevo, not HQ of Bosnian Herzegovina command, UN installation, and I faxed to The Hague, the Dutch staff here, the army staff, to what's called in that day is called Crisis Staff. That was a part of the Dutch army staff concerning Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. My idea was, and my request was, publish this and give it a name and make it raw. Tell the world what is happening and/or could happen, I should say, and that we know who is taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was the purpose achieved --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. Within the UN structure, nothing was done with it, and here in The Hague, the staff officer, Colonel, received that list, didn't understand it, said he had contact with DutchBat on the very evening that the list was received, but nobody could give him an answer, and it vanished in a well-known drawer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please turn to the last page of it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And tell us whose signature you see on it. And if you can move it again onto the machine.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I miscounted it, because afterwards it turned out to be 251. Sorry for that. But in total, the signature is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you bring the list also to the attention of the existing or perhaps even the whole list to the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I told, as far as I recollect, to Colonel Jankovic that I registered the men, without giving him the list, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did he make a comment to you about it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. He said to me something like: Okay. They are POWs, so no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did perhaps at this day or later Jankovic indicate a number of POWs which were under the protection of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Not at that occasion, because this -- I reported that I registered the men must have been on the 13th. But later on he told me that they already had 6.000 POWs, because he in fact was the first that really informed me about the breakout of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, leaving this subject and moving back to the refugees. You told us a couple of minutes ago that you discussed their situation with your doctor.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And he said that these people may die of exhaustion, I believe you said. Now, during that period while the refugees were there, did people die, and of what causes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: How many exactly died, I don't know, but we buried 11 people in the back of our base. There were children amongst them, who died probably by -- but I don't know exactly. I don't know the exact medical information. But who died by exhaustion or by what is called dehumidification, a lack of water. Two elderly people who died by exhaustion, there were two wounded who had -- impact of weapon systems, died on the base. But exactly how many outside, et cetera, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you receive reports that somebody committed or tried to commit suicide?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There were two reports on that. One man tried to jam his head with a stone, which did not succeed. And one of my lieutenants cut somebody loose who hanged himself. He was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you also get reports about nine bodies that were found shot somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who gave you this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Nine bodies was reported to me by Lieutenant Koster.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know about -- more about the cause of death of these nine bodies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. They were -- the bodies laid more or less in a row and they were absolutely -- they were executed. It couldn't have been from by combat or fire. They were in a row shot in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could be shown, please, Exhibit number 78, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On this aerial imagery, could you please indicate, if you may, the location of these nine bodies as they were pointed out to you at that time.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It should have been in this area, sir, that meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's in the middle of the picture, to the right, where we see these accumulation of, I guess, trees. And perhaps you could even mark it, taking a blue pencil, I think just -- there is one. If the usher could be of help.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Yeah. You want it marked on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You just drew a circle. Now, did you also receive the report of an execution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. One of the soldiers of my Charlie company was on post in the area outside base and reported an execution of a civilian by two Bosnian Serb soldiers. It was in the area of the bus station, north -- sorry - south of the bus station, outside of our little parameter. But he saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of the soldier?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. The soldier was Groeneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you take that seriously, what he reported to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember in what condition the soldier himself was when he reported that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I didn't -- he didn't report to me directly. He reported in his company line, so I got the report through the OPs room of Charlie Company. I saw him later on, and didn't come in any reports to me that he was dysfunctioning or something like that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are there many Groene's in Dutch names? I think the company commander of Charlie Battalion was called Groene?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: B Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: B Company. And you just said this was called Groene --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: -- veld.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Groeneveld. Could it also be Groenewegen or you can't tell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Could be. I'm sorry, but it's pretty long ago. Yeah, it's correct. Groenewegen is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to a last subject, the 17th July, 1995. Did you run into a delegation consisting of several people, and who were these people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Delegation was present at base concerning the taking over by ICRC of the 59 wounded I described to you before. And it was Colonel Jankovic, that was a lieutenant colonel who said he was a lawyer, there was a civilian who later on proved to be the new mayor of Srebrenica, Major Nikolic, and another guy who -- probably a bodyguard or something like that, of Major Nikolic. And on my side I had my adjutant, that's an NCO, Rave, myself, and I had members of my reci [phoen] platoon in the area itself just for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what was this visit about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The visit was about the transfer of the wounded to the ICRC and there should have been make appointments to pick up wounded who were in the hospital in Bratunac. ICRC would take them to a safe area and in that way make sure that those people were safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now the witness should be shown the next exhibit. That's Exhibit P79.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a list made by representative of Medecins Sans Frontieres, the list of the 59 wounded I spoke to you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you look at the date of birth, what's your observation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Generally, elderly people, sir, if I look. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, what was the role of Major Nikolic in that group?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was present, but Colonel Jankovic was clearly in charge. And it popped up that the Serbs wanted a statement from the committee and was represented by Mr. Mandic, who took part of that meeting later on. That everything during the evacuation was performed according to international law and humanitarian law, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a second. What's the link between the wounded people and this declaration you are now talking about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, it was made clear between the lines to me that the signing of that declaration would be not a condition, as it is, but in fact determine the things to happen to the 59 wounded, proceeded further on with the 59 wounded. Colonel Jankovic made that clear to me, and again between the lines, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Among these 59 wounded, were there soldiers, and what happened to these?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Major Nikolic had made the demand that he could check the wounded to check whether there were potential combatants in them. When we were -- we ended the meeting, there would be an inspection of the wounded. I said: Okay. But the ICRC consented in it. And Colonel Jankovic didn't make much of it. He said: Well, is that necessary? But Major Nikolic insisted sir, to have that inspection. And the consequence was that seven men were pointed out as being soldiers.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: They were brought to Bratunac and stayed in Bratunac. ICRC told me that they would monitor them. But -- and it's a side jump, but we had, when the further -- former transport of wounded failed, a couple of them stayed in Bratunac and we had one of our surgeons stay with them to make sure that they were treated as wounded. And when the seven men were brought to Bratunac, there was nothing wrong, but the surgeon was called away for arranging or something and when he came back he said the men were gone, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where in Bratunac did these seven people stay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The local hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was the name of your doctor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Colonel Schouten, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the wounded, the list of 59, minus the seven people you said did not return?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, they returned -- they came safely into Bosniak area, Bosniak territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a moment ago that you had to sign a declaration of -- on that day. And if you could be shown the Exhibit P36, 1. That's an English and a B/C/S translation. Perhaps if you could explain us what these two documents mean, why do we have an English translation of the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the -- in fact, it was a statement by the representatives, as you see in the first line, of the civilian authorities of the enclave. They requested me to sign as a witness, and in that request, the condition for the 59, as I mentioned before, was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps just briefly for identification purposes: You see now on the ELMO, in the middle, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who asked for this English translation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I did, because it was presented to me in the Croatian language, and I don't speak or can't read it. So I said: Stop it. We have it translated before. Because Mr. Mandic, one of the representatives, the only one who was present, because the lady, Camila Perkovic, was a patient in the MSF hospital. She had a total nervous breakdown. And Mr. Ibrahim Nuhanovic left before with his family. And Mandic asked advice. I said: Stop. We'll have it interpreted, or translated, I should say, by my own interpreters. That is done and that's the reason why there is an English version, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, perhaps the B/C/S original is also lying on the ELMO. If you could move that into the middle. Did you sign both documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, after I had my interpreters check that the contents were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And if you could help us. The date of this declaration?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: 17th of July, 1995, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's briefly go through a couple of points. If you can refer back to the English translation. In the middle of the paper, there is a little hyphen, and then it goes on and I quote: "The civilian population can remain in the enclave or evacuate, dependent upon the wish of each individual." Is that a real statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As it is, it's a real statement, but it's more or less a joke, how cynical that may sound. These people didn't have a choice. Staying in a small area with no means to survive, controlled by the Serbs, being afraid and as lethargic as they were, that is not a choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me quote you the next paragraph: "In the event that we wish to evacuate, it is possible for us to choose the direction of our movement and have decided that the entire population is to evacuate to the territory of the county of Kladanj." What's your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In fact, in the sentence, we wish to evacuate, it was not an option, so the wish is not very relevant. Secondly, they did not decide that the population, the entire population, is to evacuate the territory of Kladanj. Mladic ordered that they could evacuate as long as it was Kladanj. He dictated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last two paragraphs, and I quote them again: "It has been agreed that the evacuation is to be carried out by the army and police of the Republic of Srpska, supervised and escorted by UNPROFOR. And after the agreement had been reached, I assert that the evacuation was carried out by the Serb side correctly and the clauses of the agreement had been adhered to." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's not correct and I tried to neutralise that by the sentence I wrote down in the end, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the sentence wrote down is above the signature something in handwriting, and it reads, I quote: As for convoys actually escorted by UN forces are concerned."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct and everybody knew that we were not escorting them and by this sentence I tried to neutralise that declaration and the very moment that I wrote that down the colonel present, being the lawyer, more or less exploded. And there was some frantic discussion with Colonel Jankovic in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you pointed out several reservations to this document. What's the value of it to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Nothing, sir. Absolutely nothing. For me, it was a way to make sure or at least make possible that my 59 wounded were carried away in a proper way and in a humanitarian way. That's the reason why I signed as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to finish off, two small items. You said earlier that you had seen or heard that Mladic was present in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On the 12th, I believe. How many times was he around, and what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The first time, that is what I refer to, on the 12th, he was addressing the people and had his soldiers give away bread and be nice to the kids, Serbian television was present and probably everybody could see that on television. Second time he was there, he wanted to speak to Colonel Karremans, and as far as I know, they have been speaking to each other at the road, Srebrenica, Bratunac, the main road going there. Where exactly they were, I don't know. And the third time, I just saw him pass. He had a Mercedes jeep, probably a Dutch Mercedes jeep. And that's when I saw him pass from the area north, in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How would you characterise his appearances then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, it's what we call a nice media operation, being a good general, looking good, being nice to the kids and calling to the refugees: Don't worry. You may all come out. We'll bring you to Kladanj. Et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You described before the break the operation at what level it was controlled and how coordinated it was. Was Mladic, who is the senior VRS figure on the ground, was he in control of that operation, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, of course. Where he appeared, everybody did what he said. But it's very unlikely that he was in control of the operation itself. Because normally in an army when the highest level is interfering with technical operations, that is an operational low level, within an hour it's one big mess, because nobody knows any more in the line who has to do what and why. So I would classify it as a media operation, his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the last item I would like to show you is Exhibit P31, and if you could tell us, if you can, who this person is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's General Krstic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And have you seen him in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him when -- for the first time I made contact to Colonel Acamovic, who was allegedly in charge of the evacuation. He was in a group of officers. He was standing in the group and in discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination? Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Franken. It's lieutenant colonel; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Blagojevic, I will be asking you some questions. I want to pick up on where you just left with the Prosecution if that's okay and then we'll double back and start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Whatever you want, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that you saw Mladic there at least two times?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was reported to me that he was there. I was not in person present, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So to be clear: You did not see him, you were told that he was there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, your client wants to take the floor. Mr. Blagojevic. THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was bothered by this expression in the name of Mr. Blagojevic. He doesn't have to do this in the name of Mr. Blagojevic. I find it rather irritating. I'm very sorry about this, and the situation is upsetting for me, considering that all this is allegedly on some legal basis, and I'm wondering what kind of legal basis can possibly exist for such a situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagojevic, let me tell you the legal basis for this. We believe that Mr. Karnavas did the cross-examination on the basis of the decisions made by this Trial Chamber, which is subject to any decisions which might be rendered by the Appeals Chamber. As we mentioned before, if there's no other decisions by the Appeals Chamber, or before any decisions rendered by the Appeals Chamber, the decisions of the Trial Chamber will stand. This is our position. I quite understand your position, and I just want you to be patient, because so far, as I know, the decision of the Appeals Chamber will be rendered very soon, because we have to move on in our case. And I promise you that this witness is the last witness from the previous group, and that this witness is just crime facts basis, crime-based witness. It does not go directly to your functions during that period. Based on this presumption, we moved on. I hope we could finish this witness today so that both parties will have some time to prepare our next witness. Having said that, Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, getting back to my earlier question: It's my understanding that it was brought to your attention that at least on two occasions Mladic was there on the scene.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was reported to me. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that time, and today, you knew then and you know today what role Mladic held within the Bosnian Serb army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how would you characterise that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was, as far as I know, one of the supreme commanders of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You say one. Was he not in fact the --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He was the supreme.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, other than perhaps a political officer above him, like the president, or the Prime Minister, he was in charge of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before coming here today, I take it you met with the Prosecution, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you've had an opportunity to review all of your statements?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the witness please make a pause. Thank you. Between questions and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you've had an opportunity to at least review what you've said in the past?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, have you also had an opportunity to look at other documents unrelated to the statements that you have given?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not concerning the documents or books or reports I have myself at home. I just got the statements I myself gave before on this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you happen to read Karreman's book, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you happen to see any videos that were made during that period? Because you indicated there was somebody there videotaping?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I know Bosnian Serb television who made some kind of a recording of the happening that he came to the red and white type and spoke to the refugees. That's what I later on saw when I was back in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But you were never shown that by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you came back to Holland, did you happen to see the video from the day before, the video footage from the day before, from the 11th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I wouldn't recollect that, sir. I've seen a hell of a lot in that period, because it was quite an item in Holland, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me describe parts of it and then it might ring a bell. It may not. It shows General Mladic walking down the streets of Srebrenica, sort of in a victory, asking, you know, his men, and giving orders to colonels, lieutenants, foot soldiers, on the spot, at the operational level. Did you happen to see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I saw that. Yeah, I recollect I saw something like that. He said something like further to Potocari, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. That's part of it. Now, to me, at least - maybe I'm wrong, but maybe you could help me out here - to me it would seem, at least at that phase, at that phase of the operation going on, Mladic in that instance is acting at the operational level, like a -- is he not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't know whether he was, but it's not a condition sine qua non so to say. If there's a supreme commander on the actual spot who says go forward, it is more or less the same message he would give by radio when he was in his HQ and the unit on the spot reported we got Srebrenica. He would give normally in line the order to go, proceed or not, so that's more or less the meaning I give to his statement there in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But he's giving the orders; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, he's supreme commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. If he orders a soldier, for instance, to go kill a civilian, would the soldier's immediate commander be responsible or would Mladic be responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer or something like that. The responsibility, yeah, well, I can't give an answer on that. The fact is that he said to his units - I don't know that were colonels or lieutenants or soldiers or whatever - he says: Go on to Potocari. That is a general order, as we give as well, as I have a company or a battalion in attack who says: I reach a certain object. He gets orders from me to go on or not. That doesn't mean that I am the leader on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Getting back to my hypothetical, though. Okay. He's giving a direct order to somebody who obviously way down in the food chain.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Could be, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was he acting at the operational level at that point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not at the tactical level, but operational level, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated that at the scene, and I'm speaking now on the 11th or 12th, probably the 12th, Jankovic was the man in charge. At least that's what was told to you, in accordance with Mladic's wishes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Jankovic, as I recollect, the first time I saw Jankovic was either late on the 12th or the 13th. The 11th I didn't see him. He showed up later on. He told me that he was the man in charge concerning the withdrawal of DutchBat -- return of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Bratunac brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know if he was a member of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not -- I asked him for what his function was and he said something like high level. He wasn't specific about that. But as far as I know he was not a member of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether he was a member of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I just told you. I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what the Main Staff is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I know what a Main Staff is. I suppose that's a staff that was stationed in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's your interpretation of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please make longer breaks for the interpretation's sake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Mr. Acamovic? Who was he with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Who was he with? What do you mean, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was he with Main Staff? Was he with --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Mr. Acamovic told me that he was a G-4 officer from Pale. That's what he said to me himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: G-4 is logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you ask him whether he was directed by Mladic or Krstic or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with Mr. -- with General Krstic at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever. I just saw him at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You saw --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I didn't even know that he was a general, because it was on a distance of about ten metres with a group of officers discussing something. So I recognised his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And before I leave this area: In your opinion, was Jankovic above Nikolic or was Nikolic above Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As I've said during my testimony, the fact where I saw them together it was clear that Jankovic was taking the lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say taking the lead --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was in fact the spokesman of the Serbian delegation on the occasion of the 17th, the situation with the ICRC. And as long as Jankovic contacted me, Nikolic was never around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But on this occasion, you're saying he was the spokesperson?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you conclude from that that Jankovic was superior to Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Jankovic introduced and was recognisable as a colonel, and it's usual in armies that colonels are superior to majors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But in this instance, as I recall from your testimony, it was Nikolic who suggested or insisted that some of the men, some of the wounded, be questioned and not be turned over; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. I said - and that's what my interpreter told me - that he insisted at the end of the meeting concerning the wounded, Nikolic said that he wanted to inspect the wounded, whether to see whether there are combatants or war criminals between them. Jankovic reacted with: Is that necessary. And Nikolic insisted. So that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The inspection, ICRC and Nikolic and his bodyguard went to the wounded. I sent along part of my reci platoon. They inspected. Nikolic pointed out seven men as being combatant, and agreed with ICRC that they could be treated as wounded POWs, so transferred to the Serbs, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to make sure I understand it, sir. At this point, Nikolic makes the decision that these seven people who are POWs or war criminals or whatever --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That they're going to stay behind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He pointed them out. Jankovic was with me in the conference room. Nikolic went on the inspection. Jankovic was not there. And my lieutenant from reci platoon reported to me, confirmed by ICRC, that seven men were recognised as combatants and being that, would be interrogated, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you said that's okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That that is -- I didn't have to say anything, because they were not my wounded any more. They were from ICRC, and ICRC said it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They told you that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But I just want to make sure: Who made the decision, as far as on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I know, to be loud and clear, Mr. Nikolic was in lead of the inspection of the wounded on a different spot where I was with Colonel Jankovic, and he decided that those seven men were whatever, POWs, combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, let's start from the beginning, if that's okay with you. Hearing your background, it seems to me you've done just about everything there is to do in the infantry.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And including you were G-2 at one point.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct as well. G-2 is intel and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Intel -- intelligence and security?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please describe to us exactly what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Security is -- well, let's start with intelligence, because to try -- to keep the story short. That is gathering, analysing and giving validation to all the information you get from your sources, and sources can be anything. And it is called intelligence, military intelligence, when a report or something, an event is confirmed by several sources. Security is -- to be short -- effect -- passive, making sure that information you have more or less secret information you have doesn't get in the wrong hands, checking personnel you have, whether they are trustworthy, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you used the word "passive."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does that mean that you don't take any action?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. No. It's probably the wrong word. I'll try to say it another way. It's more the subject is, for instance, the unit itself. Being G-2 of a brigade, I was responsible for the security of the brigade. That means the security within the organisation, so documents, communications, secure communications. But personnel on key functions as well, that they were trustworthy. And the choice of tactical locations, whether they were secure enough in the sense of groups present, terrorism, things like that. And that's what I meant with passive. It's more introvert. And intelligence is an action without -- it goes -- your area of interest is outside your unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, would you please show us the relevance of those questions. It seems to us that it is out of the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Nikolic shared a like position, or at least in title, and it is going to become relevant when Mr. Nikolic testifies, both on direct and cross-examination. I just want to make sure, through the gentleman, that, you know, what his structure is vis-a-vis the structure of the VRS army at the time and under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: They are not necessarily the same, because different countries have different, you know, systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask one or two more questions, Your Honour, and then move on to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In your capacity, who was your -- as G-2, who was your supervisor, your superior officer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Brigadier, the commander of that brigade are where I was G-2, sir. But it's not applicable in the situation in Bosnia, because I was not G-2 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Okay. Just to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's all right. Did you have a separate chain of command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Separate chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, would you report on security matters, bypass your own brigade commander --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's not in the rules?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Unless it concerns my own brigade commander, but that's hypothetically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, you indicated that your mission, you had three particular missions in Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And on the one was the demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that aspect was a failure before you got there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was a joke when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. A joke. It was a failure as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, but those were basically your terms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That you were being laughed at in fact by the local --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Population --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In that sense it was a joke, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And part of the reason was because you were incapable of really exercising that part of your mandate because you weren't getting cooperation, say, from the local police?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes and no. The basic fact, basic problem was that I couldn't enter private houses, and local police, when they showed up, when we called for it, they didn't find anything, and most of the time what happened as well is that they didn't show up because we couldn't reach them. And in that situation, everybody was -- the locals were, broad smile, of course, looking in my direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And there were areas in fact within the enclave that you couldn't even go to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Where I could go or could not go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could not go.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. The Bandera Triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And why is it called the Bandera Triangle?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The area was locally named Bandera. It has the shape of a triangle, so we called it the Bandera Triangle, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact that's where you and other Dutch soldiers were captured and you were a POW for a while; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I was blocked for a while, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When you say blocked, you were captured?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I was held to a position, but without being under the direct control of the ABiH. It was -- I retreated on an OP and we were blocked there. So you could say - what's the correct word? - as far as I'm concerned, yeah, in fact, blocked. I couldn't move out of that spot. But it was now Bosniak military or representatives of the 28th Division keeping these prisoners by arms or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that Lieutenant Colonel Karremans had to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had to negotiate your release and the release of others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In order for you to be unblocked and moved out of the area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So while you were blocked you were forced to be in one particular area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were forced by the Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These were the same people that you were there supposedly to protect?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: To make sure that they were demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it, since you were blocked, they were armed, and that's how they were blocking you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. I led the first patrol myself and I was stopped by about 40 armed Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the arms were pointed in your direction to make sure that you don't unblock yourself?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, it's time for a break. Is that the right time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a fine time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we took our break, I believe I was discussing the issue of your mission and demilitarisation. On direct examination, you indicated that there was a collection point; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That collection point existed before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so there were weapons there before you got there. But for all intents and purposes, those weapons were pretty useless, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: They were partially useless, because the 28th Division did, how do you call it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Smuggle?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, no. Just hold. I'm looking for the word. Just hold, please. Was doing -- what do you call it? Well, keeping them in good condition, the small arms, the ones they were allowed to clean them, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The tank was motor -- technically still a tank. There was, as far as we knew, no ammunition, and the weapons in the weapons collection point were kept in good order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But while you were there, shipments were coming in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We don't know exactly. What happened is, and probably you mean that, is the so-called pony express.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Those are your terms, but --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. There was a route, I told just in my testimony I gave a location where there was an ambush and the route to Zepa, we call that a pony express, because once in a while, regularly, a kind of, what do you call it, a convoy of 10 to 12 packing ponies, manned with -- went in the direction of Zepa. But whether they brought back weapons, I don't know. We tried to catch them, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And there was also the famous helicopter landing; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The famous helicopter landing was a report by one of my OPs that there was helicopter movements by night. We never actually found out where they landed. I looked for it several patrols -- myself. We found an area where the trees were chopped, but never found proof of an actual helicopter landing. The Bosnian Serb Army had a helicopter place in the area of Zvornik but we never got proof they were BSA helicopters or actual helicopters of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But apparently sometime in April or May, the Muslim army there had new uniforms and also had Kalashnikovs that looked brand new. You're shaking your head.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct. We discovered in April, starting May, that there were new combat dresses apparently available to the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, but they also had Kalashnikovs --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That were brand new --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, right before the fall of Srebrenica, as I understand it from the previous statements that you have given, the Muslim army was given an opportunity to retrieve some of the weapons at the collection point, and they declined because, in accordance with your opinion, they didn't need them because they had what appeared to be modern, better, functioning equipment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand your previous testimony from one of your statements, you've given a ballpark figure of about four to four and a half thousand Muslim soldiers being part of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: While you were there, I take it, you didn't have any contact -- or did you have any contact with Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We had contact with Naser Oric the first few months we were there, because suddenly he was -- he disappeared. He was away. He was gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, all right. You say "we." Did you in particular, you personally, have contact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I had contact with him on two or three occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it that was in an official capacity, you representing the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that at their headquarters, which didn't have anything?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Twice in the post and telegraph building and once on our base when the supreme UNPROFOR commander was visiting us. And on request of Oric he had contact with the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand your testimony, there was also another building or another house where they used it as headquarters or they had -- obviously the one was for sure for DutchBat, to show that we have nothing here, and the other one was --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the other location when I visited -- I already stated that - didn't look like a headquarters to me, but it was a location they used for their staff, where their staff members were at that time present, the ones I knew. And there was a normal house in the area of Pale, and that was the communications centre. There were communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And When you're talking about Pale --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Pale within the enclave, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So not the RS Pale.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I just want to make sure. Now, from listening to you, it seemed that everybody was more or less cheating when it came to the borders.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There were three different opinions: the UN, BSA opinion, and a Muslim opinion. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And at times, that was a point of friction?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, in one particular area, it was a point of friction because of a particular factory that was located there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's in the surroundings of Observation Post Echo, in the first Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Now, that was the first observation post to more or less fall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not more or less. Fall, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you for correcting me. All right. So you lost that, but that occurred prior to the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the beginning of June, the 8th of June, with November [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, please make a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. I'm trying to discipline myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One of the reasons that area was a point of contention was because the Serbs were complaining that the Muslims were going there and raiding or looting the factory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: They were stealing wood, et cetera, from the factory. That's correct. At least, because there was a discussion whether this was a Muslim factory or a Serb factory. So for the Muslims, it was a Muslim factory, so they were not stealing. For the Serbs, it was a Serb factory, so they were stealing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: And happily, the UN border, the UN confrontation, ran amidst through that factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so by the taking over of OP Echo, it sorted of pushed the border so that the factory now was in Serb-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Correct. Well, it was still in UN territory, of course, but we didn't have the control of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, there is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I agree with you on that. Now, at some point on the humanitarian side, you attempted - you meaning the DutchBat - attempted to organise some trading between the Serbs and the Muslims, trading, that is, of humanitarian goods, food, and what have you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the opposition that you ran into was the Muslim black marketeers, who were more or less also the commanders of the Muslim army there; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: You say black marketeers, but I know that the leadership of the 28th Division had his problems with the trade in fact, and we suspected them of black market practices. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you say the leadership, we're talking Naser Oric --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: And his staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And his staff. You were asked a question to give your opinion as to why the demilitarisation did not fully -- was not fully accomplished, and why the Muslims held on to their arms. And I believe you indicated because of their wish for self-defence. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. If you take the status quo, what is the situation, you have a small area, absolutely isolated, with one of the two parties officially demilitarised, so weaponless. Potential threat on the outside and very small battalion, which even didn't have the order to defend them. So I can understand -- not justify, but understand why they kept weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of course it was the UN that decided the size of the UN mission over there; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just to make sure: You were there for not to peace-make but to --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Peacekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Peacekeeping?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: What I call combat power of the Blue Helmets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So the rules of engagement are rather restricted as to when you can use --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Self-defence. I'm rather curious. You indicated that while you were there, you noticed or you were -- you learned of two particular incidents with respect to Muslims going out and committing atrocities upon the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Wouldn't that be counter-intuitive to self-defence? In other words, you're trying to keep the Serbs from coming in. How could going and burning a village and killing innocent Serbs, how was that a form of self-defence for the Muslims that are inside the enclave hiding behind the skirts of the UN and DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I can be very clear about that. Nothing to do with it. We know in military what we call offensive action with limited target. In defence you can act offensively, but not in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would it be a form of provocation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, wasn't it a point of contention between the Serbs in your meetings with them that the UN was more or less giving safe harbour to Muslim fighters who were going out, committing atrocities, and then running back into the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is used as a statement, or an argument by the Serbs regularly. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, and in fact in some ways it's rather correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The fact is that when they went out of the enclave, do a raid with whatever target or whatever objective whatsoever, and then returned behind our Blue Helmets, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, while you were there, you had an opportunity to meet with two particular officers from the VRS that were more or less liaisoning between you and I guess the Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. They were liaisoning between me and BSA, so VRS, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And those were Nikolic and I believe the other gentleman was --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Colonel Vukovic. So one was a major, the other one was a colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I recall your earlier testimony before the break, the colonel outranks the major?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, still so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And so it would seem to me that the major would be below the colonel; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But in fact, what you saw from your dealings, it was your impression that Nikolic was in charge, and not the colonel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's not completely correct conclusion. Mostly we saw them apart from each other. Nikolic was the one who was the actual liaison, because we had contact to him most of the times, when we had contact. There was one occasions when I saw them both, as I already stated, was a meeting at OP - sorry - Observation Post Romeo, at the confrontation line. There was Colonel Vukovic and Major Nikolic together, and that was concerning the Echo problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And from that meeting, is it not a fact that you concluded that Nikolic was --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: By that occasion he took the lead, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He took the lead. Now when you say -- see, this is the second time you use that term, "took the lead." I don't know if this is a term of art or just an expression.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Let's explain what I mean. When there are a colonel and a major together speaking, and a colonel hardly says anything or doesn't make statements or doesn't ask, and the major takes the initiative in asking and negotiating, et cetera, that's what I mean, taking the lead. Not the fact that the major says to the colonel "shut up" or something like that, but actual, as a fact, he was the one who acted as the spokesman on that moment, in the presence of the colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is that the normal procedure?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that would be because the colonel outranks the major in that -- in fact, and -- let me back up. On that particular meeting, that was a rather significant meeting, was it not, the topic of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was it not rather contentious in nature?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry? Contentious?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A heated -- the topic itself was a burning issue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was a hot issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And you would expect on that kind of a hot issue, that the person with the highest rank --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- if he wants to convey the message of the top brass, would be doing the speaking, and not the lower fellow?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we talked briefly about Colonel Acamovic. As far as I understand, from listening to your testimony and reading your statements here, this particular colonel was in charge of the transportation on the scene in Potocari, I believe on the 12th --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way -- how he identified himself to me, that he was responsible for the evacuation, and as I stated before, being from G-4 Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: And this time Pale with an outside [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you happen to see him along with Colonel Jankovic, together, or were they separate occasions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Mostly I saw them separate. Once I saw them together. There was again a request for transport vehicles of the battalion, and then Jankovic -- Acamovic put the question and Jankovic was present, was at the gate of our main base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From your observations, who was in charge, or who was the superior: Acamovic or Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: There were no -- let's say the situation was not that kind that could see who is in charge or what. There was -- I was called to the gate, Acamovic was there with his request, Jankovic was present, standing along. So there was not an occasion that I could see he's in the lead or he is in the lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But it kind of struck you a bit funny that Colonel Acamovic was a low-key individual?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. A low-key individual?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I've read one of your statements where you indicated that you were rather taken aback that here was this man who was mild-mannered, and he was a colonel, and he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I was wondering: Was that because of your -- you had some particular image of how a Serb officer would behave and act?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, no, no. First, I think there are all kinds of mild mannered and kind Serbs, I suppose. No. His personality was modest. That's what I meant to say. Not an iron man, et cetera. That's the way he performed, he discussed, he asked his questions, Colonel Acamovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about Jankovic? Was he modest or immodest?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was modest. He was modest in the sense that he stayed polite, yeah, presenting the officer, the standard officer, the image we have of an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Professional?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And acted professionally?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you brought to his attention the list that you had of all the men, his demeanour was one of nonchalance, you know, non- -- so what?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In other words, you put him on notice?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the reason that you put him on notice was you wanted to let him know that there was an accounting of all these individuals, and if anything were to happen to any of them, he, and his superiors or his subordinates would be held accountable?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he gave the appearance on that particular day, and we're talking when, the 12th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The 13th. On that particular day, he gave the appearance of: Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, he was -- he took into account as a message: Okay. So what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Now, was it a fait accompli that you had already faxed it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you communicate that fact to Colonel Jankovic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. I informed him on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. What I'm saying - excuse me - on the 13th, when you informed him, did you say: By the way, this has been faxed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I told him that I reported this, the list, to my higher echelon in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did he ask for the list?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Had he asked for the list, would you have provided it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But he didn't seem concerned about the list at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you draw a conclusion from that at that particular moment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, his general position was from the very beginning that he had nothing to do, at least he said to me that he had nothing to do with the evacuation, et cetera, et cetera. So I explained his attitude from the fact that he was not busy or had not his task within the evacuation. So probably he said: Okay. Not my piece of cake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And later on, if I understand you correctly, it was later on that he informed you that they had in their possession approximately 6.000 POWs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And if I also understand you correct, based on your understanding of international law and military procedure, to separate the able-bodied men who could, in theory, be soldiers, the separation to question them, as far as you're concerned, that's proper?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's proper, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, as I believe I read somewhere, and I can dig it up here, you've already indicated in a previous statement or testimony that it was very difficult to distinguish who was active and who was inactive or who was just a civilian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: - when it came to men.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because potentially anybody from 16 to 60, in theory, was a Muslim fighter, and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Potentially a Muslim fighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And in fact, even though they were not in uniform did not mean that they were not a Muslim fighter; it just meant that they didn't have a uniform on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As I already said, it was very difficult to recognise by uniform who was part of the 28th Division or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So some of them could have been in plain clothes, and at the same time be soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You also indicated that on the Serb side it was pretty difficult also to distinguish at times, at least where they came from, because they were dressed in all sorts of different uniforms, and manners, and what have you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Most part what I call the informer statements second and third echelon, that's the units that followed up to the unit that performed the attack from Papa, were not really recognisable as a unit or something like that, by discipline and by dress, uniforms, all kinds of military outfit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it it was then difficult for you to distinguish which brigade they came from?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Or if they were in fact part of a brigade or if they were volunteers or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I did not know what the -- except from the units, as I described before, performed that armoured support, that infantry attack. It was very difficult to recognise to what unit or whatever a unit they belonged. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was Jankovic in fact, Colonel Jankovic, who you had apparently complained at one point and had indicated to you that he could not control everybody?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. That's about my last complaint about the robbing vehicles and weapons, et cetera, of my own equipment. He said: Yeah, we're doing our best, but I can't control all militia, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And this was the man who, as far as you were concerned, was Mladic's representative at the scene in the highest position at that point in time in Potocari during those days?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Concerning DutchBat and the retreat of DutchBat, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And your request to him or your complaints to him were with respect to that -- to DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You talked a little bit about the negotiations that went on, or the discussions that went on on the evening of the 11th and on the morning of the 12th. You're shaking your head. For the record --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was a yes. I don't want to be giving orders, but --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Probably you won't succeed, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you were not present there at any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
