utterances.text: So, but I take it you being the number 2 --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were getting your debriefing from your number one, which is Lieutenant Colonel Karremans?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as far as you understand it, sometime on the night of the 11th it became clear that there was going to be an evacuation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as I understand from reading some of your previous statements, at one point - and I believe this might have been on the 11th - the UN - and it might have been General Nicolai - had asked you to defend Potocari, and then two hours later to assist with the evacuation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Two hours later, but not to assist with the evacuation, to make sure that the evacuation was performed as correct as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, is it --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: And that's again sometimes partial -- well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Go ahead. No.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I missed a word, but that's the essence of my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, it's my understanding from your previous statements that the UN was asked to assist in the evacuation, and your understanding was that the UN refused or didn't have the capability, and I'm not saying DutchBat, I'm saying the UN now.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's when Mladic decided that he would do the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether there was any contact Mladic in the direction of UN. I know that on the evening of the 11th, the possibility was analysed by General Nicolai, and that is HQ BI Bosnia-Herzegovina command - that's a UN facility - to have it performed by UN, and the answer was, I heard that Mr. Colonel Karremans, that UN was not capable or -- to do that. And the suggestion was the battalion did it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So the offer was, as I understand it, from your understanding from having the discussion with Lieutenant Colonel Karremans was that the UN was given the opportunity to perform the evacuation, but Lieutenant Colonel Karremans told you that the UN, based on his contacts, told him that they were unable --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So it wasn't, it wasn't that Mladic said: I don't want the UN involved. But rather, when the UN could not step up to the plate and carry out that function, Mladic said: I will do it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's your understanding?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I understand, yes, that's the information I got from the colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's in fact what you've indicated before the parliament regarding the issue of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if I understand you correctly, on the third meeting, which would have been on the 12th, Lieutenant Colonel Karremans comes back, he's in the process of debriefing you, telling you that sometime that early afternoon the buses will arrive, and all of a sudden they came.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's around 11.00 in the morning or so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: A bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A bit later.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Before noon or so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah, somewhere around 12.00, half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And as I understand it from your testimony, all of those vehicles - trucks, buses, cars, whatever they were - were civilian and not military?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as I've seen, there were no military trucks. It was all civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did you notice that they came from different enterprises?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Some of the trucks, there was no identification of an enterprise, but on buses there were names of firms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So would it be correct, at least -- and I don't want you to guess, but I mean, did it seem at the time that these civilian vehicles and trucks had been mobilised or had been called into mobilisation by either the military or some higher authority?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: In some way they concentrated them. That's quite clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But at the time, fuel was not available from the DutchBat to give to them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Regarding this humanitarian crisis that existed there, if I can call it that -- can I call it that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. It's your understanding that you had food for -- I believe you said 800 people, for a couple of days?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I still had 800-day rations for a single person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So and it appeared to you that the rations were going to run out in a couple of days or three days?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not a couple of days. My own battalion could eat about two days of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: And I had to feed about 30.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So, and it was a humanitarian crisis that needed to be dealt with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand from your testimony, at one point you indicate that the folks that were there, the women and children, what have you, voluntarily entered the buses. Do you recall making that statement in front of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was the first time that the buses appeared, as I told you before. There was a rush for of buses. Before that time, General Mladic already said to them: You can go out, et cetera, et cetera. And there was a big rush for the buses by people who wanted to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, as I understand, you've indicated to the parliament that they voluntarily got onto the buses because they wanted to get out.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it was at some other point --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me say something about voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Again, in my former statement I earlier said voluntarily, of course, but they had no alternative, of course, so in that respect, it was voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it you made that qualification before the parliament?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Voluntarily --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You made that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Within the same context, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you told them that at the parliament or you do not recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't know, but I literally used that word, voluntarily," because there was no other choice, but in the total of my statement there, it was obvious, given by me that there was no alternative. The only thing we could do was get them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now we're talking about what we could do?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. The only choice they had, in fact, was, seeing the position, the fear they had, et cetera, is they could get out, they were very willing to get out. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And they voluntarily got on the buses?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's what you testified to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, there was food back in Srebrenica probably, was there not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The city itself, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was still in the UNHCR depot still food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the 28th Division? Did they not hoard all of the food and in fact were they not only engaged in the black marketeering and but with holding food from their own population, own people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. What we know and what we protested and corrected in a former phase is the fact that the 28th Division took his part of the food brought in by UNHCR. That's correct. But as far as I know, it was never all the food, but what they needed for that division, they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And there was -- well, they were also selling it on the black market?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Whether the division did that or not we saw the rations they got from the UNHCR, that kind of rations was sold on the black market, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You said at one point, as I understand, the DutchBat had some problems with fuel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Some problems, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Naser Oric didn't have any problems with fuel, did he?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: At least he couldn't provide me in the amount I had, I needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, but he could provide for himself and his people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you don't -- you didn't see him walking as opposed to riding in his --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I saw him once in a while. I saw him walking and I know he had a small jeep and they used within our side regularly a small truck, a blue truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, regarding the "White House", as I understand it, you got some reports from UN -- what is it, the --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: UN, United Nations military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Those are the people dressed in white?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. There was another mission, but same mission, same --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: They were in normal uniform, but, so in battle dress, but with a -- what do they call it on your arm?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: A badge?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: A badge and they were known as a mouse on the Serb side and on the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And I take it the armband was there to sort of give notice that they're there and --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. On their car, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, and I don't want to put any words in your mouth, but would it be fair to say that a lot of the intelligence that you received with respect to the "white house" came from them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Half of it. In the beginning, when I -- the only one that we were posted over there, the information came from them. Later on I posted my own men over there, when it decreased or got worse, let's say, and I got reports of my own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you sent somebody over there basically to sort of monitor the situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And keep you abreast?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you were there at the same -- you were there on the scene as well, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I've been there twice on that scene, but most of my time I was in HQ OPs room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, occasionally you would go out because, from listening to you, you really, as a commander, and I take it you were in all essence a commander there at the time, even though Karremans was there, both of you were, you know, -- or you were assisting the commander?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You need to go out, you need to go out because raw data coming into the OPs room is not necessarily complete?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. But text doesn't only cover the situation, in fact. Text gives you an indication, and then it's very good to go on the ground yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And occasionally you would go on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At one point you indicated that you were told to stop the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I was asked to stop the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were asked. And you were asked by one of the representatives or one of the -- the Muslims that became a representative at -- I believe it was the third meeting. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. The committee already was established on the evening of the 11th, because Mladic wanted those representatives on the second meeting. The first one was 2000 hours was just DutchBat were there. The second one, this committee was present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was there a particular reason why he had indicated that he wanted you to stop the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because he heard noises from the "white house" as well, and there were a hell of a lot of rumours, of course, within the refugees. And he feared that all the men would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did -- do you know whether he expressed any wishes of Sarajevo, that, in other words, that he had been in contact with higher authorities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not him. I tried all night long with Mr. Mandzic to reach the government representative of the government in Sarajevo, but we couldn't reach him, because he was not available. Mr. Mandzic came with that request that he wanted to brief or to talk with his government about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could have one moment here just to make sure that I covered everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you see Nikolic around that time, the 12th, 13th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. The first time I saw Nikolic was, I think, on the 14th, afternoon, or the 15th, when he came to the camp by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have a conversation with him, since you already knew him, or did you just see him and then you went about your business?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. He came not on some kind of a visit. He came with a purpose. And I believe on that occasion he came in with the car of our former technician. On the occasion of - what was it ?- oh, yeah the bill for the building the UNMOs rented had to be paid and he tried to have DutchBat pay for the cost of -- made by the Bosnian Serb army for the POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did he inform you who had instructed him, or was he there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. No. He announced that he came. He asked that he could come on the base with his car. I allowed him that, so he parked in front of the HQ. And then we spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And did he ask you -- did he throw a particular figure at you, how much the rent was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, he didn't come that far. As far as the UNMOs were concerned, I told you before, they were not -- they didn't belong to DutchBat, so I said: Okay. I'll have the UNMOs make contact with you about that thing. And I told him that it's absolutely ridiculous. Let me pay for POWs they took. And he didn't insist further on, so I never heard the math.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether he want cheque, cash, a credit card?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The discussion didn't come that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And as far as you know, or as far as you recollect, he didn't say: I've been ordered by Mladic --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I've been ordered by my commander, I've been ordered by General Krstic. He just showed up?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He showed up --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Looking --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It had to be arranged, still had to be arranged, and it appeared that these two items were at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. One last question. You indicated that at one point you had requested to meet with the commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. That was the wish of my commander, Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you pass that wish on or --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. It was passed by -- passed on by our S-5, our liaison to -- I suppose it was Major Boering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as far as you know, nothing happened?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, the meeting didn't take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether that wish was communicated, actually communicated, to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I was not present, but normally when we say to an S-5, you have to do that and that, I suppose he does. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. But normally we inspect. I didn't check it I wasn't present and whether it was given through in the BSA lines, I don't know, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you have a time, an approximation when this request would have been made?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. As I recollect correctly, at least one was made after the report from the Serbs about the Muslim raid in the north of the enclave. That's the phase in which my colonel said -- I think we have to talk to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. And if he wants us to do something about it, we'll have the correct information. We want to go to the spot, et cetera, et cetera. That was, as far as I recollect, the reason for his request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have any contact with a Colonel Beara. That was Nikolic, okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One last housekeeping matter. You said that Nikolic showed up in a car with a former technician.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: We had a civilians doing jobs on the base for us normally and one of them was a man called Rizo, family name I don't recollect. He was an engineer of the battery factory in peacetime. And he knew exactly how all the electrical wires, et cetera, which we used, of course, so he was in our service to maintain things like that, et cetera, et cetera. In the end phase, when we were registering all UN personnel, et cetera, because they could go out with the battalion, as the battalion went out, Rizo disappeared -- he had a light blue Japanese car which he asked if he may park that on the base. And Rizo was gone. Although he knew that he could come with the battalion. The story from the refugees was that Rizo had made a deal with the Serbs. We never saw him again until Major Nikolic came with the car of Rizo on our base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who was driving it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Major Nikolic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that gentleman was Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That gentleman was Muslim, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examination, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you: When was it that you arrived in Srebrenica for your mission in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The 15th of January, 1995. Personally I arrived then, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that your first mission in Bosnia or have you been to any other areas in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. Not in Bosnia. It was not my first mission, but not in Bosnia. In Bosnia it was my first mission, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So the very first mission in Bosnia in general?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that in January 1995 you took over the duty from the DutchBat that you called DutchBat number 2?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the takeover of duty, were you informed by them that the area that they -- during their mandate was not demilitarised in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That is correct too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that on that occasion during the takeover of duty, did they also tell you that they estimated that it was -- there was approximately 4.000 to 5.000 troops and weapons pieces that were still remaining in the enclave at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct as well. They used the number 4.500, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Considering your experiences as an intelligence officer and the period of time that you spent there, which is from the 15th of January until the second half of July, did you conclude that their estimate was correct and that it was more or less an accurate piece of information you were given by them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. We never came to that figure, but we -- the other way around: Tried to find confirmation of that figure. And there was no item or no facts that would lead to another figure. That's correct. So we -- it was confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said today that one part of the Srebrenica enclave, and up to the south-west, what you called the Bandera Triangle, you said that this was an area where you did not have under your control under your direct control. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is the consequence of that fact the blockade that you were under, that you mentioned while you were answering the question put to you by Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not directly. We got permission of our supreme commander, sector north-east, UN occasion, to press hard to restore freedom of movement in the Bandera Triangle, and the way we did that was commanding up a couple of patrols, which the first patrol to go in I led it myself and the confrontation with the BiH forces in that area, the consequence there of that was that I was blocked by about four days. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So is it correct to conclude that you practically did not have freedom of movement in that area, and you were not able to know about the troop movement and the weapons of BH army in that area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's not completely correct. We did not have freedom of movement in that area. That is correct. But the locations OP Alpha, Charlie, and to new locations we made in the south, Kilo and Delta - that's Observation Post - did permit us to have some control. But the problem with all the observation posts was that the UN wanted them showing the flags, so we had to put them on the top of a hill, make them white, et cetera. So we did not control, for instance, all kinds of valleys or something like that, bush valleys, in between those posts. But in general, we had some control over the complete area. But again, it was possible to go in and out of the enclave without seeing the locations on our strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, that was the meaning of the question, considering the data that the Defence has at their disposal. So was it possible in that area that you did not have under your control, was it possible to have artillery pieces, mortars, as well as APCs, without you actually noticing that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: At the very moment that they would have been used, we would have noticed that. We noticed that there was probably some mortar equipment in that area. We don't have any indication that there were APCs or real artillery. But we could not, in that area, not pick them up and get them out and bring them to the WPC, weapon collection point. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So it is possible, is my conclusion correct, that it is possible that these weapons were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It's a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the report that you submitted to the NIOD -- I'm not quite sure what the abbreviation stands for, but in the interview that you had before the parliamentary commission, you said, among other things, that many blue berets, many members of the DutchBat, had the feeling that the Muslims did not wish to have their protection and that they were abusing the presence of the DutchBat in order to conduct illegal military operations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: When you mean with the Muslims, the 28th Division, then that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am particularly talking about the 28th Division. When I say, "members of the BH army," I mean the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Okay. Just because the attitude of the civilian population was quite different. They were generally very happy that we were there. We had problems with the 28th Division in our operations. That's absolutely true. The very moment that there was a problem with the Serbs, for instance, when they claimed they came further forward into the enclave there was coordination and discussion with them and all kinds of other moments, not. And with them, I mean 28th Muslim Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did those facts that they were conducting illegal military operations, you mean what you already said, that is, to carry out offensive operations onto Serb territory from inside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. At least two occasions we knew about that, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And those two times, do you also include those two incidents that you mentioned in April and May 1995, that is, the killing of seven Serb soldiers on the way to Zepa, as well as an attack on a Serb village which was burnt down? And the name of that village is Tresnjica, or something similar.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the two incidents I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You personally, or anyone else from the DutchBat, did you conduct control, that is, did you have insight into the attack on these villages, or any other attacks, how many villages, how many houses were attacked and burnt during the period while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Now, the first question is did we conduct control. Now, the situation was that our observation posts were on the top of the hills, white-painted, and by night, with lamps on it. That was the order from the UN. We had to be very visible. So military scene, it was an absolutely insane location, which meant that all the valleys or - what do you call them? - ravines, deep terrain between the hills by night. Anyway, we didn't control that. Then you asked me if we -- insight. We do have insight on the consequences of these attacks. No. As I already stated before, in the case of the raid on -- in the north of the enclave, we asked to go out of the enclave and check out what happened, and we were not allowed by the BSA. I think that is the answer on your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to conclude that all of these incidents were chronologically took place before the attack on the Srebrenica enclave that you said took place on the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The incidents were before the attack on Srebrenica enclave, but the final attack on the Srebrenica enclave is not on the 6th of July, as mentioned by you. It was later, of course. But probably -- the first action was 6 or 8 June on OP Echo, and final attack on the enclave started around the 8th, with -- after two days of shelling of OP Foxtrot, taken over by OP Foxtrot. But anyway, in essence, it is correct that the mentioned incidents were before the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: They were before. Very well. Thank you. You spoke about the fact that you noticed - and this is still again the attack on Srebrenica [sic] - you noticed new uniforms and new army equipment worn by the BH troops. Do you have any idea how that happened and how were BH army members supplied with army equipment and new uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: As far as we said, we saw, that is before the attack, of course, but I see it wrong here on my screen. But new uniforms, yes, new equipment, the only thing we saw was new updated Kalashnikovs, small arms. And the idea how it happened, there are a couple of possibilities, but it's speculation possibility is that actually helicopter landings took place, which we tried to find out but didn't get confirmed. And the other way is, as mentioned, pony express from Zepa. Those are possibilities, but I have no idea further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did all this take place before your talks about the joint defence with the army of B and H of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: If you mean the identification of new equipment, new Kalashnikovs and new uniforms, that was before we had that discussion about who is doing what when the Serbs attack. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you understand by this, who is doing what, and when, to defend the enclave? Do I understand correctly that this was a division of roles in the protection of the defence lines, the protection of both from the Serbs, or is it something entirely different?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It is, as I said before by statement, it is different. The question was: What is DutchBat doing when the Serb army will attack the enclave? The answer was: Defend their OPs. And during that discussion, it was said by the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division that if they took the terrain between the OPs, there would, without having the bearings of a coordinated defence, but there would be a kind of defensive ring around the enclave. That's what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly that practically the area between the observation posts held by DutchBat were to be taken over by the forces of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No. There was no area between the observation post to be held by DutchBat, because our mission was not to defend the enclave. Our mission was to deter by presence. That's why we had these almost ridiculous locations for our observation posts. So it was a question of being taken over by the BH army they were not allowed to take over our observation posts. The only Dutch element in that so-called ring would be our own observation post and I was entitled within my mandate to defend my observation post, because then I would fight in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was precisely my question. So they would take the areas between the observation posts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: They suggested that when they would take the areas between the observation posts, then a kind of ring would come to exist. Sorry. I missed a word but I try to tell it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let us go back for a moment to the talks about opening up trade and the flow of goods between the enclave and the Serb-held territory. You said that these talks failed and that you concluded that this was not in the interest of certain individuals from the 28th Division. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, the talks didn't fail, because there was an agreement with the civilian leadership, but later on they came back on it and said that there were internal problems which did not allow to. The fact that it was not in the interest of certain individuals is a personal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "civilian structures," you mean within the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the major -- the mayor, I should say, of Srebrenica, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you gain the impression that the Serb negotiators were willing to open up trade and to make use of the experience they had from Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yes. Moreover, as far as I recollect, it was on the initiative of the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will simply try to clarify some points now from your testimony. You mentioned the Main Staff several times. You said that there was a Main Staff at Pale, that he belonged to. When you say "at Pale," are you referring to the staff representing the political leadership, that is, Radovan Karadzic, as president of the staff, or the military that were part of the Main Staff? Or to put it differently, the man we are speaking about, who did he represent? Jankovic, Acamovic, were these leaders from Pale or from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The last part. I meant the military staff, highest level within the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about a place called Han Pijesak, and do you know it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I heard it. I recognise it. But I can't connect it to an event. Sorry it's familiar to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You can't -- can you connect it with the headquarters of the Main Staff? Do you believe that the headquarters of the Main Staff was at Pale?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: What that concerns: Colonel Acamovic said he came from Pale and was a G-4 officer. Colonel Jankovic never told me where he came from, but I suggested that he was from the same level. So I have those two in connection with the location Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Today you also said that you saw the arrival of General Mladic and that he had a Mercedes jeep, which was probably Dutch. How did you reach this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I saw not his arrival, but I saw this jeep pass. It had all the small typically Dutch issues on it. We have a blackout lighting to drive by night, et cetera, and we are in that form the only nation who has it. It was on his jeep. So that's for me the possibility that it was a Dutch jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you think, but you are not sure, that it was a jeep taken from DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: That's why I said probably, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said today at one point that coordinating evacuation was carried out at corps level and perhaps at the level of the Main Staff. Referring to the people whose task it was to organise the logistics of the evacuation. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Yeah. I said that -- I was asked for an opinion on what level it should have been done in my point of view, and that's when I said: The highest staff available, to prevent discussing whether the Main Staff or staff is in Pale or in Han Pijesak, as you said. Anyway, that's the level I meant. Probably the highest level within the BSA has to coordinate an action like that, if you have to, for instance, concentrate all that transport from the whole of the area. It's almost impossible for, for instance, a corps who has a limited area to get it done. That was the intention of my remark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely my point. You saw Mladic there, you saw General Krstic there, you saw Jankovic and Acamovic, representatives of the Main Staff, and from all this, you drew the conclusion that the level of organisation had to be at corps level or at the level of the Main Staff; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The fact that I saw Mladic, I explained that before how I see that. I saw a man back in Holland and asked to testimony within the Krstic process I recognised as apparently being General Krstic, because at the very moment I saw him, I didn't know it was General Krstic. And by the fact that those two colonels told me, at least Acamovic told me that he came from Pale, G-4, was for me an indication that my idea about the level that had coordinated, it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To put it simply, I am not a soldier, but please try to answer me anyway. We have a Main Staff, we have a corps, who, in your view, is in command at that point in time, heading this whole operation about the evacuation of the population.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, a corps could do it when he had some - what do you call it? - possibility to command in the region of another corps, and otherwise it has to be a coordinated next highest staff, and that means Main Staff. And probably you have to make the difference between the military operation being the attack on Srebrenica and the evacuation. It is possible that the attack has been led by a corps, a military corps, and then the operation evacuation is coordinated on a higher level, because of, well, reasons, as I gave you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May I conclude, then, that the evacuation could not have been organised by a brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, what could or not could -- in my opinion, it's very unlikely that a brigade organised the complete evacuation. Mind you, organise it. I don't say perform it. It's something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now conclude with the following: From what you said today, I conclude that it is correct that the Srebrenica area was not demilitarised; that in the Srebrenica area, there were about four and a half thousand armed members of the army of BH; that there was an area in the Srebrenica protected zone that was not fully under your control; and that it's possible that there were heavy weapons there; and that the attack on the Srebrenica area was chronologically preceded by two events that you mentioned, the burning of a village and the murder of seven soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska; and that the civilian leadership did not agree to opening up the flow of goods and trade between the Srebrenica area and the Serb-held territory. Is this conclusion correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Please, one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's -- I'm not saying that my learned counsel is misstating the facts, but it's a lot what he puts to this witness at the end of his cross-examination. So if he could make this compound question, put it into pieces, if he really needs it, because it seems like a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, I think a different counsel has a different style. Earlier the counsel did not make such kind of sum-up, because there's a danger to mischaracterise what the witness told us. So I hope you could withdraw this question and that the Bench could come to this kind of conclusion, when we're deliberating the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not my intention to bring the witness into a position where he says something that is not correct. I was simply trying to sum up everything that has already been answered. And as the transcript contains the answers to each of these questions, I have no problem in withdrawing this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any redirect, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, only three questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would just like to start where my counsel left off. You said that it was unlikely that the brigade would organise the whole evacuation. But then you said performing is something else. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I already said my arguments -- I gave my arguments why I think that it has to be -- the preparation has to be done by a pretty high level, has to do with areas of responsibility and the possibility to give orders into a direction or to an organisational element. But then again, if it is organised, transport, coordination has been about the route to take, a brigade can perform it, can actually execute the conclusion of the preliminary preparation of the higher level. So what I mean to say that corps did prepare it, but the manning of the buses and the actual process, let's say, let's name it that way, can be done by a brigade, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in fact, to conclude: It needs to be done by somebody. The people who coordinate, the names mentioned - Latic [phoen], Jankovic - you didn't really see these people driving vehicles, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The second issue, the humanitarian crisis, you gave -- in fact, you were asked by Mr. Karnavas whether you agreed with his characterisation of a humanitarian crisis, and in fact you gave a number of instances, the suicides and hygienic situation and so on. Then you said that people voluntarily boarded the buses because, as you put it, they had no alternative, given the situation. Clarify, please: Who was responsible for these humanitarian crises? Who caused it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: It was caused, in fact, by the Serbs. The situation was not too nice in the enclave before the attack. That's quite clear. But we could cope with it. And after the attack, that situation increased significantly. Because bringing together so many people in this weather, it was about 35 degrees centigrade, and the food and medical situation known by the Serbs, they knew exactly what our logistics situation was. Yeah, well, then it's quite clear: Caused by the Serbs, first by the attack; secondly, what we call convoy terror. In fact, they controlled exactly what anybody, UNHCR or the UN brought in the enclave. We had to ask permission and report very detailed what was in trucks coming into the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question: You were asked about your complaints in relation to - you just mentioned it - convoy terror. You raised these complaints with Colonel Jankovic, and he said, according to you, and I quote you: "We are doing our best, but I can't control," I think you said," all militia, et cetera." Now, did you buy this explanation from Jankovic that he wasn't -- he couldn't control these people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: No, but the discussion was not relevant because he said -- the fact was that he couldn't control and he said that he would do his utmost to get the equipment back, and that's the end of it, I can say, and do it better, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So did you believe he could do better, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I think if they absolutely wanted, they could have arranged it and organised it, at least the most of our equipment we could become back. But it was obviously not an issue or it was not in the interests to give it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions by the Judges? Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant Colonel, was the DutchBat personnel in position to escort the convoys with the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we tried, but it proved to be that we were not in the position. As I stated, We were stopped and robbed, et cetera, with all different kind of reasons. So when I lost about 16 vehicles and a hell of a lot of men - at least, I did not have the position of them - we had to stop, because I was out of small vehicles, et cetera. It was practically not possible any more, not seeing the fact that the quality of the escort was minimal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did you know where the refugees have been taken to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: The refugees we knew, because our first convoys -- the first convoys had been escorted, and I got reports from the escorts where they were taken to. Then I found out that they had to dismount quite far from the confrontation line, and I was informed about the route they had to take through the confrontation line into BiH territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what happened to the refugees?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: When they arrived in their, so to say, own area, they were brought to Tuzla and they were brought into a huge camp with tents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You stated that you have contacted Mr. Momir Nikolic. What was the role of Momir Nikolic in the events in and around Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: He was the acting liaison, so all questions or remarks or complaints I had in the direction or concerning the Serbs, and especially the Bosnian Serb army, I had to communicate that through him. Formally, it was Colonel Vukovic, but he was not around, suddenly available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Have you ever contacted Mr. Vidoje Blagojevic, Dragan Jokic, and Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm looking for the last name, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: Not as far as I know, sir. The name doesn't call a face, et cetera, for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: You said that you have read the book "Srebrenica: Who Cares?" written by Colonel Karremans. What is your assessment of this book?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT FRANKEN
utterances.text: I wouldn't have written it in this style, sir, but the actual facts, et cetera, are facts as mentioned in that book. I hope that is an answer, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of Judge's question? Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? On the Prosecution side?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, there are, Mr. President. And looking at the list which was, I believe, given to the court deputy, it's P75, P76, P77, P78, P79, and P80. All the other exhibits were tendered by previous witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there any objections? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those documents are admitted into evidence. Are there any documents on the Defence side that they would like to tender through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to give your evidence. I think we benefitted a lot from your testimony. The usher will show you out of the room. We wish you good luck.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may go now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as I said, that according to our original plan, we'll hear next witness on Wednesday morning, unless, unless, there is a further notice. So the -- yes, Mr. Karnavas. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Does that mean that the further notice could be ready for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't know. I hope so. I'm not predicting, you know, what kind of notice it is. But I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess my question was, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- is there a possibility that we would have a session tomorrow, or is it the earliest would be on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think tomorrow will be free.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
